deliberate targeting | Between 1639 and 1652, [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland") was involved in the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"), a series of conflicts which included the [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), the [Irish Rebellion of 1641](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"), the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), the [Irish Confederate Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Confederate_Wars "Irish Confederate Wars") and finally the [conquest of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwellian_conquest_of_Ireland "Cromwellian conquest of Ireland") and the [subjugation of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Scottish_war_/(1650%E2%80%931652/) "Anglo-Scottish war (1650–1652)") by the English [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army"). Within Scotland, from 1644 to 1645 a Scottish civil war was fought between Scottish [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier")—supporters of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") under [James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquess_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose")—and the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"), who had controlled [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") since 1639 and who were allied with [English Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead"). The Scottish Royalists, aided by Irish troops, had a rapid series of victories in 1644–45, but were eventually defeated by the Covenanters. The Covenanters then found themselves at odds with the English Parliament, so they signed [the Engagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Engagement_/(1647/) "The Engagement (1647)") with Charles I in 1647 and supported him in the [second English civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_civil_war "Second English civil war"). Following Charles' execution, they received and crowned his son [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") at Scone and thus stated their intention to place him on the thrones of England and Ireland as well. In 1650, Scotland was invaded and occupied by the New Model Army under [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"). Origins of the war – wars in three kingdoms ------------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Origins of the war – wars in three kingdoms")\] The war originated in Scottish opposition to religious reforms imposed on the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland") (_[the Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_/(word/) "Kirk (word)"))_ by [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). This culminated in February 1638 when representatives from all sections of Scottish society agreed a [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant"), pledging resistance to liturgical 'innovations.' An important factor in the political contest with Charles was the Covenanter belief they were preserving an established and divinely ordained form of religion which he was seeking to alter. The Covenant also expressed wider dissatisfaction with the sidelining of Scotland since the [Stuart kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_monarchs "Stuart monarchs") became monarchs of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") in 1603, while the Kirk was viewed as a symbol of Scottish independence.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackieLenmanParker1986204%E2%80%93205-1) [![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/EDI_CITY_CAC_1978_113.jpg/250px-EDI_CITY_CAC_1978_113.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EDI_CITY_CAC_1978_113.jpg) The Signing of the [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant") in [Greyfriars Churchyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyfriars_Churchyard "Greyfriars Churchyard"), 1638 by [William Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hole_/(artist/) "William Hole (artist)") Victory in the 1639 and 1640 [Bishops Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Wars "Bishops Wars") left the Covenanters firmly in control of Scotland but also destabilised [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Ireland "Kingdom of Ireland") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). Widespread opposition to Crown policies meant the [Parliament of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") refused to fund war against the Scots, leading Charles to consider raising an army of Irish Catholics in return for abolishing the [penal laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_laws_/(Ireland/) "Penal laws (Ireland)") against them. This prospect alarmed his enemies in both England and Scotland; when the Covenanters threatened to provide military support for their co-religionists in [Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster "Ulster"), it sparked the [Irish Rebellion of 1641](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"), which quickly degenerated into massacres of [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") settlers in Ireland.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2004146%E2%80%93148-2) The Covenanters responded in April 1642 by sending [an army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter_Army_in_Ireland "Covenanter Army in Ireland") to Ulster led by [Robert Monro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Monro "Robert Monro"), which engaged in equally bloody reprisals against Catholics. Although both Charles and Parliament supported raising troops to suppress the rebellion in Ireland, neither side trusted the other with their control. A struggle for control of military resources ultimately led to the outbreak of the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") in August 1642.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton20035%E2%80%936-3) Scottish Royalists and Covenanters ---------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Scottish Royalists and Covenanters")\] [![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg/250px-1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg) [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquess_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose"); a Covenanter general in 1639 and 1640 who became leader of the Royalist campaign 1644–1645 The [Scottish Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Reformation "Scottish Reformation") established a kirk that was [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity") in structure and [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism") in doctrine. By 1640, less than 2% of Scots were Catholics, concentrated in places like [South Uist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Uist "South Uist"), controlled by [Clanranald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clanranald "Clanranald"), but despite its minority status, fear of [popery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Catholicism "Anti-Catholicism") remained widespread.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFissel1994269,_278-4) Since Calvinists believed a 'well-ordered' monarchy was part of God's plan, the Covenanters committed to "defend the king's person and authority with our goods, bodies, and lives" and the idea of government without a king was inconceivable.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacleod20095%E2%80%9319_passim-5) This meant that unlike England, throughout the war all Scots agreed the institution of monarchy itself was divinely ordered and hence why the Covenanters supported the restoration of Charles I in the [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War"), then his son in the [Third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_English_Civil_War "Third English Civil War"). Where Covenanters and Scottish Royalists disagreed was the nature and extent of Royal authority versus that of the people, including through the popularly governed Presbyterian church; the relative narrowness of this distinction meant Montrose was not unusual in fighting on both sides.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201553%E2%80%9354-6) Royalism was most prominent in the [Scottish Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Highlands "Scottish Highlands") and [Aberdeenshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeenshire "Aberdeenshire"), due to a mix of religious, cultural and political reasons; Montrose switched sides because he distrusted Argyll's ambition, fearing he would eventually dominate Scotland and possibly depose the King.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7) Furthermore, the [Gàidhealtachd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A0idhealtachd "Gàidhealtachd") was a distinct cultural, political and economic region of Scotland. It was [Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Gaelic_language "Scottish Gaelic language") in language and customs and at this time was largely outside of the control of the Scottish government. Some Highland [clans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clans "Clans") preferred the more distant authority of King Charles to the powerful and well-organised [Lowlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Lowlands "Scottish Lowlands") based government of the Covenanters. Clan politics and feuds also played a role; when the Presbyterian [Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Campbell "Clan Campbell"), led by their chief, [Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), sided with the Covenanters, their rivals automatically took the opposing side. It should be said some of these factors overlap that spanned the Irish Sea: for instance, the MacDonalds were Catholics, were sworn enemies of the Campbells, and had a strong [Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaels "Gaels") identity. Historian David Stevenson writes: "It is a moot point whether one should call the MacDonnells of Antrim Scots or Irish... To the MacDonnells themselves the question was largely irrelevant, they had more in common with native Irish and Scots Highlanders, with whom they shared a common Gaelic language and culture than with those who ruled them".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson20058-8) The Irish intervention ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: The Irish intervention")\] Montrose had already tried and failed to lead a [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") uprising by 1644 when he was presented with a ready-made Royalist army. The [Irish Confederates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_Ireland "Confederate Ireland"), who were loosely aligned with the Royalists, agreed in that year to send an expedition to Scotland. From their point of view, this would tie up Scottish Covenanter troops who would otherwise be used in Ireland or England. The Irish sent 1500 men to Scotland under the command of [Alasdair MacColla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alasdair_MacColla "Alasdair MacColla") MacDonald, a MacDonald clansman from the [Western Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Isles "Western Isles") of Scotland. They included [Manus O'Cahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manus_O%27Cahan%27s_Regiment_/(English_Civil_War/) "Manus O'Cahan's Regiment (English Civil War)") (an Irish cousin to MacColla) and his 500-man regiment. Shortly after landing, the Irish linked up with Montrose at [Blair Atholl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blair_Atholl "Blair Atholl") and proceeded to raise forces from the MacDonalds and other anti-Campbell Highland clans. The new Royalist army led by Montrose and MacColla was in some respects very formidable. Its Irish and Highland troops were extremely mobile, marching quickly over long distances – even over the rugged Highland terrain – and were capable of enduring very harsh conditions and poor rations. They did not fight in the massed [pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_/(weapon/) "Pike (weapon)") and [musket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musket "Musket") formations that dominated continental Europe at the time, but fired their muskets in loose order before closing with swords and half-pikes. This tactic was effective in such a wilderness and swept away the poorly trained Covenanter militias that were sent against them. These locally raised levies frequently ran away when faced with a terrifying [Highland charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland_charge "Highland charge"), and were slaughtered as they ran. However, the Royalist army also had major problems: the clans from the west of Scotland could not be persuaded to fight for long away from their homes – seeing their principal enemy as the Campbells rather than the Covenanters, which resulted in fluctuating membership – and the Royalists also lacked [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry"), leaving them vulnerable in open country. Montrose overcame some of these disadvantages through his leadership and by taking advantage of the forbidding Highland mountains. Keeping his enemies guessing where he would strike next, Montrose would sally out to attack lowland garrisons and withdraw to the Highlands when threatened by the more numerous enemy. In the safety of the mountains, he could fight on terrain familiar to his army, or lead the Covenanters on wild goose chases.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood199867-9) The year of Royalist triumph and collapse ----------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: The year of Royalist triumph and collapse")\] [![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg/250px-The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg) Archibald Campbell, Covenanter and Chief of the Campbell clan From 1644 to 1645 Montrose led the Royalists to six famous victories, defeating covenanting armies larger than his own of roughly 2000 men (except at Kilsyth, where he led approximately 5,000).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7) In the Autumn of 1644, the Royalists marched across the Highlands to [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Scotland "Perth, Scotland"), where they smashed a Covenanter force at the [Battle of Tippermuir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tippermuir "Battle of Tippermuir") on 1 September. Shortly afterwards, another Covenanter militia met a similar fate [outside Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Aberdeen_/(1644/) "Battle of Aberdeen (1644)") on 13 September. Unwisely, Montrose let his men pillage Perth and [Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen "Aberdeen") after taking them, leading to hostility to his forces in an area where Royalist sympathies had been strong. Following these victories, MacColla insisted on pursuing the MacDonald's war against the Campbells in [Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyll "Argyll") in western Scotland. In December 1644, the Royalists rampaged through the Campbells' country. During the clan warfare [Inveraray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inveraray "Inveraray") was torched and all armed men were put to the sword; approximately 900 Campbells were killed.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTECowan1995176-10) In response to the attack on his clansmen, [Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll") assembled the Campbell clansmen to repel the invaders. Montrose, finding himself trapped in the [Great Glen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Glen "Great Glen") between Argyll and Covenanters advancing from [Inverness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverness "Inverness"), decided on a flanking march through the wintry mountains of [Lochaber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lochaber "Lochaber") and surprised Argyll at the [Battle of Inverlochy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Inverlochy_/(1645/) "Battle of Inverlochy (1645)") (2 February 1645). The Covenanters and Campbells were crushed, with losses of 1,500. Montrose's famous march was acclaimed as "one of the great exploits in the history of British arms" by John Buchan and [C. V. Wedgwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._V._Wedgwood "C. V. Wedgwood").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood199882-11) The victory at Inverlochy gave the Royalists control over the western Highlands and attracted other clans and noblemen to their cause. The most important of these were the [Gordons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Gordon,_3rd_Marquess_of_Huntly "Lewis Gordon, 3rd Marquess of Huntly"), who provided the Royalists with [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry") for the first time. Inverlochy was an important strategic victory for the Royalists, because the Scottish Covenanter army in England was ordered to send a proportion of their force north to help bolster the Covenanter forces in Scotland. This significantly weakened the Scottish army in England and it was only the lack of Royalist infantry and artillery in the north of England that prevented [Prince Rupert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Rupert "Prince Rupert") from attacking them. In April 1645, to hinder the northwards movement of English Royalist field artillery, [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") [led a cavalry raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War#Cromwell's_raid "First English Civil War") into the English Midlands. The raid was the first active operation carried out by the newly formed [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911P._412_%C2%A7_%22Rupert's_Northern_March%22_and_%22Cromwell's_Raid%22-12) [![Image 23](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Alexleslie.jpg/250px-Alexleslie.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexleslie.jpg) [Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie,_1st_Earl_of_Leven "Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven"), Lord General of the Covenanter Army In April Montrose was surprised by [General William Baillie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Baillie_/(soldier/) "William Baillie (soldier)") after a raid on Dundee, but eluded capture by having his troops double back on the coast road and fleeing inland in a corkscrew retreat. Another Covenanter army under [John Urry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Urry_/(soldier/) "John Urry (soldier)") was hastily assembled and sent against the Royalists. At [Auldearn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auldearn "Battle of Auldearn"), near [Nairn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairn "Nairn"), Montrose placed Macdonald and most of the infantry in view of the enemy and concealed the cavalry and remaining infantry. Despite Macdonald attacking prematurely, the ruse worked, and Urry was defeated on 9 May. Another cat-and-mouse game between Bailie and Montrose led to the [Battle of Alford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Alford "Battle of Alford") on 2 July. Montrose confronted the Covenanters after the latter had forded the [Don](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Don,_Aberdeenshire "River Don, Aberdeenshire"), forcing them to fight with the river at their back and on uneven ground. The Royalists triumphed and advanced into the lowlands. Bailie went in pursuit and Montrose waited for him at [Kilsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kilsyth "Battle of Kilsyth"). During the ensuing battle the Royalists were inadvertently aided by Argyll and other members of the "Committee of Estates," who ordered Bailie to make a flank march across the front of the Royalist army, which pounced on them and triumphed. After Kilsyth (15 August), Montrose seemed to have won control of all Scotland: In late 1645, such prominent towns as [Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee "Dundee") and [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow") fell to his forces. The Covenanting government had temporarily collapsed, paying for its over-confidence in defeating Royalist resistance. As the royally commissioned lieutenant-governor and captain-general of Scotland, Montrose used his powers to summon parliament to meet in Glasgow, but the limitations of his triumph soon became clear. King Charles was in no position to join the Royalists in Scotland, and though Montrose wanted to further Royalist objectives by raising troops in the southeast of Scotland and marching on England, MacColla showed that his priorities lay with the war of the MacDonalds against the Campbells and occupied Argyll. The Gordons also returned home, to defend their own lands in the northeast. During his campaign, Montrose had been unable to attract many lowland royalists to his cause. Even after Kilsyth few joined him, having been alienated by his use of Irish Catholic troops, who were "regarded as barbarians as well as enemies of true religion." Additionally, his covenanting past "left lingering mistrust among royalists."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7) Montrose, his forces having split up, was surprised and defeated by the Covenanters, led by [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie,_1st_Lord_Newark "David Leslie, 1st Lord Newark"), at the [Battle of Philiphaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Philiphaugh "Battle of Philiphaugh"). Approximately 100 Irish prisoners, having surrendered upon promise of quarter, were executed, and 300 of the Royalist army's camp followers – mostly women and children – were killed in cold blood.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTECowan1995237-13) MacColla retreated to [Kintyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintyre "Kintyre"), where he held out until the following year. In September 1646 Montrose fled to Norway. The Royalist victories in Scotland had evaporated almost overnight owing to the disunited nature of their forces. The end of the civil war in Scotland ------------------------------------ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: The end of the civil war in Scotland")\] The [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") had ended in May 1646, when [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") surrendered to the Scottish Covenanter army in England. After failing to persuade the King to take the Covenant, the Scots finally handed him over to the commissioners of the English Parliament (the "[Long Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament")") in early 1647. At the same time they received part payment for the service of their army in England, which then returned north. In 1646, Montrose left for [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), while MacColla returned to Ireland with his remaining Irish and Highland troops to re-join the [Confederates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_Ireland "Confederate Ireland"). Those who had fought for Montrose, particularly the Irish, were massacred by the Covenanters whenever they were captured, in reprisal for the atrocities the Royalists had committed in Argyll. Scotland and the Second Civil War --------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Scotland and the Second Civil War")\] [![Image 24](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Oliver_Cromwell_by_Samuel_Cooper.jpg/250px-Oliver_Cromwell_by_Samuel_Cooper.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oliver_Cromwell_by_Samuel_Cooper.jpg) [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"). When the Covenanters' alliance with the English Parliament broke down, Cromwell invaded Scotland and conquered the country Ironically, no sooner had the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter "Covenanter") defeated the [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") at home than they were negotiating with Charles I against the English Parliament. The Covenanters could not get their erstwhile allies to agree on a political and religious settlement to the wars, failing to get [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") established as the official religion in the Three Kingdoms and fearing that the [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") would threaten Scottish independence. Many Covenanters feared that under Parliament, "our poor country should be made a province of England." A faction of the Covenanters known as the [Engagers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers "Engagers"), led by the [Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton"), therefore [sent an army to England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_invasion_of_England_/(1648/) "Scottish invasion of England (1648)") to try to restore Charles I in 1648. However, it was routed by [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell")'s [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") at the [Battle of Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_/(1648/) "Battle of Preston (1648)") and annihilated at the [Battle of Winwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Winwick "Battle of Winwick"). This intervention on behalf of the King caused a brief civil war within the Covenanting movement. The most hardline Presbyterians under the Earl of Argyll rebelled against the main Scottish army under [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_/(Scottish_general/) "David Leslie (Scottish general)"). The two factions came to blows at the [Battle of Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stirling_/(1648/) "Battle of Stirling (1648)") in September 1648, before a peace was hastily negotiated. Charles was executed by the [Rump Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament") in 1649, and Hamilton, who had been captured after Preston, was executed soon after. This left the extreme Covenanters, still led by Argyll, as the main force in the Kingdom. ### Montrose's defeat and death \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Montrose's defeat and death")\] [![Image 25](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Arms_of_Montrose.png/250px-Arms_of_Montrose.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Montrose.png) A grisly souvenir of Montrose's hanging: His right arm (seen front and back) and sword In June 1649, [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquess_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose") was restored by the exiled [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") to the now nominal lieutenancy of Scotland. Charles also opened negotiations with the Covenanters, now dominated by Argyll's radical Presbyterian [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"). Because Montrose had very little support in the lowlands, Charles was willing to disavow his most consistent supporter to become a king on terms dictated by the Covenanters. In March 1650 Montrose landed in [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney "Orkney") to take the command of a small force, composed mainly of continental mercenaries, which he had sent on before him. Crossing to the mainland, Montrose tried in vain to raise the clans, and on 27 April he was surprised and routed at the [Battle of Carbisdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Carbisdale "Battle of Carbisdale") in Ross-shire. After wandering for some time he was surrendered by [Neil Macleod of Assynt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_MacLeod#17th_century_&_Civil_War "Clan MacLeod"), to whose protection, in ignorance of Macleod's political enmity, he had entrusted himself. He was brought a prisoner to [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), and on 20 May sentenced to death by the Parliament. He was [hanged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging "Hanging") on the 21st, with [Wishart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wishart_/(bishop/) "George Wishart (bishop)")'s laudatory biography of him put round his neck. To the last, he protested that he was a real Covenanter and a loyal subject. Anglo-Scottish war, 1650–1652 ----------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Anglo-Scottish war, 1650–1652")\] Despite their conflict with the Scottish Royalists, the Covenanters then committed themselves to the cause of Charles II, signing the [Treaty of Breda (1650)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Breda_/(1650/) "Treaty of Breda (1650)") with him in the hope of securing an independent Presbyterian Scotland free of Parliamentarian interference. Charles landed in Scotland at [Garmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garmouth "Garmouth") in [Moray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moray "Moray") on 23 June 1650 and signed the 1638 Covenant and the 1643 Solemn League immediately after coming ashore. The threat posed by King Charles II with his new Covenanter allies was considered to be the greatest facing the new English Republic, and [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") left some of his subordinates in Ireland to continue [their conquest of the island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwellian_conquest_of_Ireland "Cromwellian conquest of Ireland") and returned to England in May. He arrived in Scotland on 22 July 1650, advancing along the east coast towards Edinburgh. By the end of August, his army was reduced by disease and running out of supplies, so he was forced to order a retreat towards his base at the port of Dunbar. A Scottish Covenanter army under the command of [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_/(Scottish_general/) "David Leslie (Scottish general)") had been shadowing his progress. Seeing some of Cromwell's sick troops being taken on board the waiting ships, Leslie made ready to attack what he believed was a weakened remnant (though some historians report that he was ordered to fight against his better judgment by the Covenanter General Assembly). Cromwell seized the opportunity, and the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") inflicted a crushing defeat on the Scots at the subsequent [Battle of Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dunbar_/(1650/) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)") on 3 September. Leslie's army, which had strong ideological ties to the radical [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"), was destroyed, losing over 14,000 men killed, wounded and taken prisoner. Cromwell's army then took [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and by the end of the year his army had occupied much of southern Scotland. [![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Cromwell_at_Dunbar_Andrew_Carrick_Gow.jpg/250px-Cromwell_at_Dunbar_Andrew_Carrick_Gow.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cromwell_at_Dunbar_Andrew_Carrick_Gow.jpg) _[Cromwell at Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwell_at_Dunbar "Cromwell at Dunbar")_, by [Andrew Carrick Gow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carrick_Gow "Andrew Carrick Gow"). The Battle of Dunbar was a crushing defeat for the Covenanters This military disaster discredited the radical Covenanters known as the [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") and caused the Covenanters and Scottish Royalists to bury their differences (at least temporarily) to try to repel Cromwell's invasion of Scotland. The Scottish Parliament passed the Act of Levy in December 1650, requiring every burgh and shire to raise a quota of soldiers. A new round of conscription was undertaken, both in the Highlands and the Lowlands, to form a truly national army named the Army of the Kingdom, that was put under the command of Charles II himself. Although this was the largest force put into the field by the Scots during the Wars, it was badly trained and its morale was low as many of its constituent Royalist and Covenanter parts had until recently been fighting each other. In July 1651, under the command of General John Lambert, part of Cromwell's force crossed the [Firth of Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth") into [Fife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fife "Fife") and defeated the Scots at the [Battle of Inverkeithing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Inverkeithing "Battle of Inverkeithing"). The New Model Army advanced towards the royal base at [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Scotland "Perth, Scotland"). In danger of being outflanked, Charles ordered his army south into England in a desperate last-ditch attempt to evade Cromwell and spark a Royalist uprising there. Cromwell followed Charles into England leaving [George Monck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Monck "George Monck") to finish the campaign in Scotland. Meanwhile, Monck took [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling "Stirling") on 14 August and [Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee "Dundee") on 1 September, reportedly killing up to 2,000 of its 12,000 population and destroying every ship in the city's harbour, 60 in total. The Scottish Army of the Kingdom marched towards the west of England because it was in that area that English Royalist sympathies were strongest. However, although some English Royalists joined the army, they came in far fewer numbers than Charles and his Scottish supporters had hoped. Cromwell finally engaged the new king at [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") on 3 September 1651, and beat him – in the process all but wiping out his army, killing 3,000 and taking 10,000 prisoners. Many of the Scottish prisoners taken by Cromwell were sold into indentured labour in the West Indies, Virginia and [Berwick, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwick,_Maine "Berwick, Maine"). This defeat marked the real end of the Scottish war effort. Charles escaped to the European continent and with his flight, the Covenanters' hopes for resisting Cromwell's invasion were dashed. From occupation to Restoration ------------------------------ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: From occupation to Restoration")\] [![Image 27](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/General_Monck.jpg/250px-General_Monck.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Monck.jpg) General Monck commanded the Parliamentarian forces that occupied Scotland during the Interregnum and led his troops to London to restore the monarchy in 1660 Between 1651 and 1654, a Royalist rising took place in Scotland.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker20052-14) [Dunnottar Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunnottar_Castle "Dunnottar Castle") was the last stronghold to fall to Parliamentarian troops in May 1652. Under the terms of the [Tender of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tender_of_Union "Tender of Union"), the Scots were given 30 seats in a united Parliament in London, with General Monck appointed as the military governor of Scotland. His troops continued to garrison Scotland for the rest of the [Interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interregnum_/(England/) "Interregnum (England)"). Sporadic Royalist rebellions continued throughout the Commonwealth period in Scotland, particularly in the western Highlands, where [Alasdair MacColla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alasdair_MacColla "Alasdair MacColla") had raised his forces in the 1640s. The northwest Highlands was the scene of another pro-Royalist uprising in 1653–55, which was only put down with the deployment of 6,000 New Model Army troops there. Monck garrisoned forts all over the Highlands – for example at [Inverness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverness "Inverness"), and finally put an end to Royalist resistance when he began deporting prisoners to the [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") as [indentured labourers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indentured_labour "Indentured labour"). However, lawlessness remained a problem, with bandits known as [mosstroopers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosstroopers "Mosstroopers"), very often former Royalist or Covenanter soldiers, attacking both Parliamentarian troops and Scottish civilians. After the death of Oliver Cromwell in 1658, the factions and divisions which had struggled for supremacy during the early years of the interregnum reemerged. Monck, who had served Cromwell and the English Parliament throughout the civil wars, judged that his best interests and those of his country lay in the Restoration of Charles II. In 1660, he marched his troops south from Scotland to ensure the monarchy's reinstatement. Scotland's Parliament and legislative autonomy were restored under [The Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_/(Scotland/) "Restoration (Scotland)") though many issues that had led to the wars; religion, Scotland's form of government and the status of the Highlands, remained unresolved. After the [Glorious Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution "Glorious Revolution") of 1688, many more Scots would die over the same disputes in [Jacobite rebellions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobite_rebellions "Jacobite rebellions"). It is estimated that roughly 28,000 men were killed in combat in Scotland itself during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms. More soldiers usually died of disease than in action at this time (the ratio was often 3–1), so it is reasonable to speculate that the true military death toll is higher than this figure. In addition, it is estimated that around 15,000 civilians died as a direct result of the war – either through massacres or by disease. More indirectly, another 30,000 people died of the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic") in Scotland between 1645 and 1649, a disease that was partly spread by the movement of armies throughout the country. If we also take into account the thousands of Scottish troops who died in the civil wars in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War") and [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Confederate_Wars "Irish Confederate Wars") (another 20,000 soldiers at least), the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms") certainly represent one of the bloodiest episodes in Scottish history. 25.content:
[55°30′28″N 4°22′49″W / 55.50783°N 4.38022°W](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir¶ms=55.50783_N_4.38022_W_type:event_region:GB) | Battle of Mauchline Muir | | --- | | Part of the [Scottish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Scotland in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms") | | [![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Mauchline_Muir_battle_site%2C_Mauchline%2C_East_Ayrshire.jpg/330px-Mauchline_Muir_battle_site%2C_Mauchline%2C_East_Ayrshire.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mauchline_Muir_battle_site,_Mauchline,_East_Ayrshire.jpg) Mauchline Muir battle site | |
Date12 June 1648
Location

Mauchline, Ayrshire, Scotland

ResultInconclusive
| | Belligerents | | [Engagers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers "Engagers") Party | [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") | | Commanders and leaders | | [John Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Middleton,_1st_Earl_of_Middleton "John Middleton, 1st Earl of Middleton") [James Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Callendar "Earl of Callendar") | [John Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Campbell,_1st_Earl_of_Loudoun "John Campbell, 1st Earl of Loudoun") | | Strength | | 800 infantry[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathieson1902-1) 1,200 cavalry | 850 cavalry[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManganiello2004347-2) | The **Battle of Mauchline Muir** was an engagement fought on 12 June 1648 between two rival factions of the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters") of Scotland. On one side were those who favoured [The Engagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Engagement_/(1647/) "The Engagement (1647)"), known as Engagers, and on the other those who were opposed to the Engagement, and known as the [Kirk party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_party "Kirk party").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_New_Statistical_Account_of_Scotland:_Ayr-Bute1845161-3) By 1646, the Presbyterian Covenanter movement had [defeated the Scottish Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Scotland in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms"), who favoured unconditional loyalty to King [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). In 1646 at the end of the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War"), Charles I had surrendered to the Scottish army which was in England fighting as an ally of the English Parliament. As part of the negotiated agreement for their payment and withdrawal back to Scotland, the Scots handed Charles over to the English Parliament and returned to Scotland in 1647.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreat_Rebellion1911-4) In the negotiations over what constitutional settlement should be implemented the Scottish Covenanters were one of four parties to the negotiations. The other three parties were Charles, the English Parliament dominated Presbyterians, and the [Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_/(religion/) "Independent (religion)") in the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army"). Charles stalled for time hoping that either his supporters in alliance with one or more of the other parties would succeed in restoring him to his throne with little or no change to his constitutional position.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreat_Rebellion1911-4) In December 1647 a faction in the Covenanters reached an agreement with King Charles known as [The Engagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Engagement_/(1647/) "The Engagement (1647)") in which he promised that if the Covenanters would support him militarily he would support the establishment of Presbyterianism in England for a period of three years. The faction known as the Kirk Party, strongly influenced by the [General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Assembly_of_the_Church_of_Scotland "General Assembly of the Church of Scotland") were opposed, arguing against an agreement which didn't include the permanent adoption of Presbyterianism and attacked the [Parliament of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland") for proceeding in matters of religion without consulting them.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurgol199863-5) In April 1648 the Engagers took control of the Scottish Parliament, and they authorised the sending of an army, under the command of [James, Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton"), south to implement the agreement. England had been engulfed in the [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") and Hamilton was joined by a force of royalists under [Marmaduke Langdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marmaduke_Langdale,_1st_Baron_Langdale_of_Holme "Marmaduke Langdale, 1st Baron Langdale of Holme").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurgol199863-64-6) In June 1648, a members of the Kirk party gathered in Mauchline to join in a celebration of the [Eucharist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucharist "Eucharist") that lasted several days.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertson1908249-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM'Kay1880150-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDouglas200867-9) Following the celebration 2,000 armed Kirk party supporters gathered on the Mauchline Moor, choosing leaders in evident preparation of making their dissatisfaction with the Engagement known.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathieson190292-10) Into the midst of this rode five troops loyal to the Scottish Parliament and the Engagement. They were commanded by [John Middleton, 1st Earl of Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Middleton,_1st_Earl_of_Middleton "John Middleton, 1st Earl of Middleton"), and [James Livingstone, Earl of Callender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Callendar "Earl of Callendar").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertson1908249-7) The Kirk party supporters had in their company seven ministers who managed to obtain assurance from the Engager leaders that if their group surrendered, there would be an amnesty.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathieson190292-10) But the majority of the Kirk party did not accept these terms. Many were eager for the fight and some 200 of the party were deserters who were excluded from the amnesty. For some time, the Kirk party supporters held their own, but when reinforcements arrived to more than double the Engager troops, the day was decided.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManganiello2004347-2)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMathieson190292-10) Though the Engagers took the day, each side of the conflict lost roughly equal numbers, with combined fatalities estimated between 30 and 40 men.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManganiello2004347-2) All seven ministers and 65 members of the Kirk party were arrested, but later freed. While the Engagers were victorious, the battle itself helped firm Scottish opposition to the Engagement. A couple of months after this small victory the Engager army commanded by James Duke of Hamilton suffered a crushing defeat by New Model Army at the [Battle of Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_/(1648/) "Battle of Preston (1648)"), and after a short civil war in Scotland the Kirk party emerged as victors (see [Whiggamore Raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiggamore_Raid "Whiggamore Raid"), the [Battle of Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stirling_/(1648/) "Battle of Stirling (1648)") and the Treaty of Stirling).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManganiello2004576-11) Subsequently, a Scottish Parliament convened in Edinburgh on 4 January 1649 and "approved the opposition" represented by those at Mauchline.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDouglas200867-9) 1. 27.content:
A Three Days' Battle
--------------------

It was through this busy Lancashire, of which we have been reading in the last chapter, that Cromwell came marching to meet the Scots. The Scots leader, the Duke of Hamilton, was a bad general. His officers quarrelled among themselves and with the English Royalists, and he was not strong enough to make them agree and do as he commanded. Each wanted to go his own way, yet there was no great man among them who could force them to act together. Indeed, he would have been a clever man who could have made Scots Presbyterians and English Episcopalians do that.

Hamilton's line of march was so long and straggling, that his army was really divided into three parts. Most of the horse was at Wigan; Hamilton himself at Preston, fifteen miles behind, and a third party at Kirby Lonsdale, in Westmorland, thirty miles still farther off, when Cromwell attacked them.

It was upon the English Royalists under Langdale, and a few Scottish horse under Hamilton, that the first shock of battle fell. For four hours they fought gallantly in the hedge-ringed fields of Preston Moor. But from hedge to hedge they were beaten back, till at last, with ranks broken and disordered, they fled towards Preston pursued by the Ironsides. Through the streets they fled, and over the bridge which crossed the Ribble, then scattering, some fled northward to carry the news of disaster to the Scottish foot; some southward to Wigan; some they knew not where. Of the army which had fought that day on Preston Moor, few indeed remained, for a thousand lay dead upon the field, and four thousand more were prisoners—"nothing hindering the ruin of that part of the enemy's army but the night," wrote Cromwell. "Where Langdale and his broken forces are I know not; but they are exceedingly shattered."

In the Scottish camp there was gloom and despair, yet the leaders were no more united than before. Some wanted to make a stand and fight where they were. Others wished to march away in the darkness and try to join the horse at Wigan. This they decided to do. They had no horses to carry their baggage and ammunition. All must be left behind. So each man filled his powder-flask, and the rest was left to fall later into the hands of Cromwell. Then, without sound of drum or pipe, in the rain and silence of the night, the already weary, hungry men began their march southward. So quietly did they go, so weary were the pursuing Ironsides, that they were already three miles on the way before Cromwell found out that they had gone. Then he started in pursuit.

While the Scottish foot were thus marching southward in the rain and dark, the horse from Wigan marched northward to meet them. They went, however, by different roads, and so missed each other. But Middleton, the leader of the horse, finding out his mistake, turned back again, and, coming between the foot soldiers and Cromwell's pursuing army, beat him back again and again.

So at last, the weary soldiers reached Wigan. They were faint with hunger, wet to the skin and covered with mud, for it had poured with rain all day and the roads were like marshes. Cromwell and his men were close behind and encamped outside the town, being "very dirty and weary, and having marched twelve miles of such ground as I never rode in all my life," says Cromwell.

But there was no rest for the weary Scots with the terrible Ironsides pursuing. Having plundered Wigan, Royalist town although it was, for food and clothes, they marched on again, hoping to reach Warrington and put the Mersey between themselves and their foes.

The heavy rainclouds now blew over, and a watery moon shone out. It shone upon those who wearily fled, and upon those who, almost as weary, pursued. Next morning at Winwick, a few miles from Warrington, Cromwell came up with the Scots. Again there was a desperate fight. Again the Royalists were defeated. Leaving behind them a thousand dead and two thousand prisoners, they continued the spiritless march. After them came the Ironsides; but the chase was nearly over. At Warrington, four thousand more surrendered to Cromwell, Hamilton and a few thousand horse only escaping. "They (the Scots) are so tired and in such confusion," writes Cromwell, "that if my horse could but trot after them, I could take them all. But we are so weary, we can scarce be able to do more than walk after them. They are the miserablest party that ever was. I durst engage myself, with five hundred fresh horse, and five hundred nimble foot, to destroy them all. My horse are miserably beaten out; and I have ten thousand prisoners."

The three days' fight named from Preston was over. "A wonderful great mercy and success," the Parliament called it. The great Royalist army of the North was utterly crushed by a force scarcely one-third its size. The fleeing remnants, one way or another, fell into the hands of Cromwell. And so the second Civil War ended, having lasted only a few months. Of the ten thousand prisoners, some were allowed to go free, after promising never again to take up arms against the Parliament. Others were sent as slaves to the plantations of Virginia and the West Indies.

26.content:
The **English Civil War** or **Great Rebellion** was a series of [civil wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_war "Civil war") and political machinations between [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavaliers "Cavaliers") and [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") in the [Kingdom of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England")[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-4) from 1642 to 1651. Part of the wider 1639 to 1653 [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"), the struggle consisted of the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") and the [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War"). The [Anglo-Scottish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Scottish_war_/(1650%E2%80%931652/) "Anglo-Scottish war (1650–1652)") of 1650 to 1652 is sometimes referred to as the _Third English Civil War._

While the conflicts in the three kingdoms of England, [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland") and [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Ireland "Kingdom of Ireland") had similarities, each had their own specific issues and objectives. The First English Civil War was fought primarily over the correct balance of power between [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") and [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). It ended in June 1646 with Royalist defeat and the king in custody.

However, victory exposed Parliamentarian divisions over the nature of the political settlement. The vast majority went to war in 1642 to assert Parliament's right to participate in government, not abolish the monarchy, which meant Charles' refusal to make concessions led to a stalemate. Concern over the political influence of radicals within the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") like [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") led to an alliance between moderate Parliamentarians and Royalists, supported by the [Covenanter Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"). Royalist defeat in the 1648 Second English Civil War resulted in the [execution of Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Charles_I "Execution of Charles I") in January 1649, and establishment of the [Commonwealth of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England").

In 1650, [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") was crowned King of Scotland, in return for agreeing to create a [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") church in both England and Scotland. The subsequent Anglo-Scottish war ended with Parliamentarian victory at [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") on 3 September 1651. Both Ireland and Scotland were incorporated into the Commonwealth, and the British Isles became a unitary state. This arrangement ultimately proved both unpopular and unviable in the long term, and was dissolved upon the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in 1660. The outcome of the civil wars effectively set England and Scotland on course towards a [parliamentary monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_monarchy "Parliamentary monarchy") form of government.

The term _English Civil War_ appears most often in the singular, but historians often divide the conflict into two or three separate wars. These were not restricted to [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") alone, as [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales") (having been [annexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_in_Wales_Acts_1535_and_1542 "Laws in Wales Acts 1535 and 1542") into the [Kingdom of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England")) was affected by the same political instabilities. The conflicts also involved wars with [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") and [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") and civil wars within them. Some historians have favoured the term _The British Civil Wars_. From the Restoration to the 19th century, the common phrase for the civil wars was "the rebellion" or "the great rebellion".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-5)

The wars spanning all four countries are known as the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"). In the early 19th century, [Walter Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott "Walter Scott") referred to it as "The Great Civil War".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-6) The [1911 _Encyclopædia Britannica_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica_Eleventh_Edition "Encyclopædia Britannica Eleventh Edition") called the series of conflicts the "Great Rebellion".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-7) Some historians, notably [Marxists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxists "Marxists") such as [Christopher Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Hill_/(historian/) "Christopher Hill (historian)"), favoured the term "[English Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Revolution "English Revolution")".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-8)

Each side had a geographical stronghold, such that minority elements were silenced or fled. The Royalist areas included the countryside, [the Shires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shire#%22The_Shires%22 "Shire"), the cathedral cities of [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York"), [Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester "Chester"), [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_England "Worcester, England") and [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford"), and the less economically developed areas of northern and western England and Wales. Parliament's strengths spanned the industrial centres, ports, and economically advanced regions of southern and eastern England, including the remaining cathedral cities. Historian [Lacey Baldwin Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacey_Baldwin_Smith "Lacey Baldwin Smith") wrote: "the words _populous, rich, and rebellious_ seemed to go hand in hand".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1983251-9)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes1985236%E2%80%93263-10)

Strategy and tactics
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=English_Civil_War&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Strategy and tactics")\]

Many officers and veteran soldiers had fought in European wars, notably the [Eighty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years%27_War "Eighty Years' War") between the Spanish and the Dutch, which began in 1568, as well as earlier phases of the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War "Thirty Years' War") which began in 1618 and concluded in 1648.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker1986-11)

The war was of unprecedented scale for the English. During the campaign seasons, 120,000 to 150,000 soldiers would be in the field, a higher proportion of the population than were fighting in Germany in the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War "Thirty Years' War").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-12)

The main battle tactic came to be known as [pike and shot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_and_shot "Pike and shot") infantry. The two sides would line up opposite one another, with infantry brigades of [musketeers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musketeer "Musketeer") in the centre. These carried matchlock muskets, an inaccurate weapon which nevertheless could be lethal at a range of up to 300 yards. Musketeers would assemble three rows deep, the first kneeling, second crouching, and third standing. At times, troops divided into two groups, allowing one to reload while the other fired.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurneYoung1998-13)\[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\] Among the musketeers were pike men, carrying [pikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_/(weapon/) "Pike (weapon)") of 12 feet (4 m) to 18 feet (5.5 m) long, whose main purpose was to protect the musketeers from cavalry charges. Positioned on each side of the infantry were cavalry, with a right wing led by the [lieutenant-general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_general "Lieutenant general") and left by the [commissary general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissary_general "Commissary general"). Its main aim was to rout the opponents' cavalry, then turn and overpower their infantry.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Simkin-14)\[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS "Wikipedia:NOTRS")_\][\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-15)\[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\]

The Royalist cavaliers' skill and speed on horseback led to many early victories. [Prince Rupert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Rupert_of_the_Rhine "Prince Rupert of the Rhine"), commanding the king's cavalry, used a tactic learned while fighting in the Dutch army, where cavalry would charge at full speed into the opponent's infantry, firing their pistols just before impact.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Simkin-14)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-16)\[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\]

However, with Oliver Cromwell and the introduction of the more disciplined [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army"), a group of disciplined pike men would stand its ground, which could have a devastating effect. The Royalist cavalry had a tendency to chase down individual targets after the initial charge, leaving their forces scattered and tired, whereas [Cromwell's cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironside_/(cavalry/) "Ironside (cavalry)") was slower but better disciplined.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Simkin-14) Trained to operate as a single unit, it went on to win many decisive victories.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-17)

The English Civil War broke out in 1642, less than 40 years after the death of Queen [Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England "Elizabeth I of England"). Elizabeth had been succeeded by her [first cousin twice-removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cousin_chart "Cousin chart"), [King James VI of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I"), as James I of England, creating the first [personal union of the Scottish and English kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_the_Crowns "Union of the Crowns").[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-18) As King of Scots, James had become accustomed to Scotland's weak parliamentary tradition since assuming control of the Scottish government in 1583, so that upon assuming power south of the border, the new King of England was affronted by the constraints the [English Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") attempted to place on him in exchange for money. Consequently, James's personal extravagance, which resulted in him being perennially short of money, meant that he had to resort to extra-parliamentary sources of income. Moreover, increasing inflation during this period meant that even though Parliament was granting the King the same nominal value of subsidy, the income was actually worth less.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-19)

This extravagance was tempered by James's peaceful disposition, so that by the succession of his son Charles I in 1625 the two kingdoms had both experienced relative peace, internally and in their relations with each other. Charles followed his father's dream in hoping to unite the kingdoms of England, Scotland and Ireland into a single kingdom.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-20) Many English Parliamentarians were suspicious of such a move, fearing that such a new kingdom might destroy old English traditions that had bound the English monarchy.\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] Because James had described kings as "little gods on Earth", chosen by God to rule in accordance with the doctrine of the [Divine Right of Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_Right_of_Kings "Divine Right of Kings"), and Charles shared his father's position, the suspicions of the Parliamentarians had some justification.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-21)

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/King_Charles_I_after_original_by_van_Dyck.jpg/330px-King_Charles_I_after_original_by_van_Dyck.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Charles_I_after_original_by_van_Dyck.jpg)

[Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") believed in the [divine right of kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_right_of_kings "Divine right of kings"); painting by [Van Dyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_van_Dyck "Anthony van Dyck")

### Parliament in an English constitutional framework

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=English_Civil_War&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Parliament in an English constitutional framework")\]

At the time, the Parliament of England did not have a large permanent role in the English system of government. Instead, it functioned as a temporary advisory committee and was summoned only if and when the monarch saw fit. Once summoned, a Parliament's continued existence was at the King's pleasure since it was subject to dissolution by him at any time.

Yet in spite of this limited role, Parliament had acquired over the centuries _de facto_ powers of enough significance that monarchs could not simply ignore them indefinitely. For a monarch, Parliament's most indispensable power was its ability to raise tax revenues far in excess of all other sources of revenue at the Crown's disposal. By the 17th century, Parliament's tax-raising powers had come to be derived from the fact that the [gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentry "Gentry") was the only stratum of society with the ability and authority to collect and remit the most meaningful forms of taxation then available at the local level. So, if the king wanted to ensure smooth revenue collection, he needed the gentry's cooperation. For all of the Crown's legal authority, its resources were limited by any modern standard to the extent that if the gentry refused to collect the king's taxes on a national scale, the Crown lacked a practical means of compelling them.

From the thirteenth century, monarchs ordered the election of representatives to sit in the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England "House of Commons of England"), with most voters being the owners of property, although in some [potwalloper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potwalloper "Potwalloper") boroughs every male householder could vote. When assembled along with the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords"), these elected representatives formed a Parliament. So the concept of Parliaments allowed representatives of the property-owning class to meet, primarily, at least from the point of view of the monarch, to sanction whatever taxes the monarch wished to collect. In the process, the representatives could debate and enact [statutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute "Statute"), or [acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_parliament "Act of parliament"). However, Parliament lacked the power to force its will upon the monarch; its only leverage was the threat of withholding the financial means required to implement his plans.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohnston190183%E2%80%9386-22)

### Parliamentary concerns and the Petition of Right

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=English_Civil_War&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Parliamentary concerns and the Petition of Right")\]

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Sir_Peter_Lely_001.jpg/250px-Sir_Peter_Lely_001.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sir_Peter_Lely_001.jpg)

[Henrietta Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Maria_of_France "Henrietta Maria of France"), painted by [Peter Lely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Lely "Peter Lely"), 1660

Many concerns were raised over Charles's marriage in 1625 to a [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") French princess, [Henrietta Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Maria_of_France "Henrietta Maria of France"). Parliament refused to assign him the traditional right to collect customs duties for his entire reign, deciding instead to grant it only on a provisional basis and negotiate with him.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGregg1984129%E2%80%93130-23)

Charles, meanwhile, decided to send an expeditionary force to relieve the French [Huguenots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenots "Huguenots"), whom French royal troops held [besieged in La Rochelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_La_Rochelle "Siege of La Rochelle"). Such military support for Protestants on the Continent potentially alleviated concerns about the King's marriage to a Catholic. However, Charles's insistence on giving command of the English force to his unpopular royal favorite [George Villiers, the Duke of Buckingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of_Buckingham "George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham"), undermined that support. Unfortunately for Charles and Buckingham, the 1627 relief expedition proved a fiasco,[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGregg1984166-24) and Parliament, already hostile to Buckingham for his monopoly on [royal patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage"), opened [impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment_in_the_United_Kingdom "Impeachment in the United Kingdom") proceedings against him.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Gregg-175-25) Charles responded by dissolving Parliament. This saved Buckingham but confirmed the impression that Charles wanted to avoid Parliamentary scrutiny of his ministers.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Gregg-175-25)

Having dissolved Parliament and unable to raise money without it, the king assembled a new one in 1628. (The elected members included [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), [John Hampden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hampden "John Hampden"),[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Adair_1976-26) and [Edward Coke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Coke "Edward Coke").) The new Parliament drew up a [Petition of Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petition_of_Right "Petition of Right"), which Charles accepted as a concession to obtain his subsidy.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Purkiss_2007_93-27) The Petition made reference to [Magna Carta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Carta "Magna Carta"),[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-28) but did not grant him the right of [tonnage and poundage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonnage_and_poundage "Tonnage and poundage"), which Charles had been collecting without Parliamentary authorization since 1625.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESommerville199265,_71,_80-29) Several more active members of the opposition were imprisoned, which caused outrage;[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESommerville199265,_71,_80-29) one, [John Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Eliot_/(statesman/) "John Eliot (statesman)"), subsequently died in prison and came to be seen as a martyr for the rights of Parliament.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussell1998417-30)

Charles avoided calling a Parliament for the next decade, a period known as the "[personal rule of Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_rule_of_Charles_I "Personal rule of Charles I")", or by its critics as the "Eleven Years' Tyranny".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-31) During this period, Charles's policies were determined by his lack of money. First and foremost, to avoid Parliament, the King needed to avoid war. Charles made peace with France and Spain, effectively ending England's involvement in the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War "Thirty Years' War"). However, that in itself was far from enough to balance the Crown's finances.

Unable to raise revenue without Parliament and unwilling to convene it, Charles resorted to other means. One was to revive conventions, often outdated. For example, a failure to attend and receive [knighthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knighthood "Knighthood") at Charles's coronation became a finable offence with the fine paid to the Crown. The King also tried to raise revenue through [ship money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_money "Ship money"), demanding in 1634–1636 that the inland English counties pay a tax for the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") to counter the threat of privateers and pirates in the English Channel.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Adair_1976-26) Established law supported the policy of coastal counties and inland ports such as London paying ship money in times of need, but it had not been applied to inland counties before.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Adair_1976-26)

Authorities had ignored it for centuries, and many saw it as yet another extra-Parliamentary, illegal tax,[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Pipes-143-32) which prompted some prominent men to refuse to pay it. Charles issued a writ against [John Hampden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hampden "John Hampden") for his failure to pay, and although five judges including George Croke supported Hampden, seven judges found in favour of the King in 1638.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Adair_1976-26) The fines imposed on people who refused to pay ship money and standing out against its illegality aroused widespread indignation.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War#cite_note-Pipes-143-32)

During his "Personal Rule", Charles aroused most antagonism through his religious measures.
