[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/The_Queen_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg/250px-The_Queen_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Queen_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg)

[Alexander Douglas-Hamilton, 16th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Douglas-Hamilton,_16th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Alexander Douglas-Hamilton, 16th Duke of Hamilton"), acting as Hereditary Bearer of the [Crown of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Scotland "Crown of Scotland"), holding the crown at the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Parliament "Scottish Parliament") before [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II "Queen Elizabeth II") and [Presiding Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presiding_Officer_of_the_Scottish_Parliament "Presiding Officer of the Scottish Parliament") [Tricia Marwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tricia_Marwick "Tricia Marwick") in July 2011

The duke of Hamilton and Brandon is the hereditary keeper of the [Palace of Holyroodhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Holyroodhouse "Palace of Holyroodhouse"), the official royal residence in Scotland, where he maintains large private quarters. He is also, as Lord Abernethy and in this respect successor to the Gaelic [earls of Fife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earls_of_Fife "Earls of Fife"), the hereditary bearer of the [Crown of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Scotland "Crown of Scotland"), a role performed by the 15th duke at the inauguration of the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Parliament "Scottish Parliament") in 1999[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-4) and the 16th duke at the State Opening of Parliament, 30 June 2011.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-5) As Hereditary Bearer of the Crown of Scotland, the 16th Duke also placed the crown upon the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II during a service of remembrance in [St Giles' Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Giles%27_Cathedral "St Giles' Cathedral") on 12 September 2022.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-BBC_NEWS-6) Traditionally, the duke of Hamilton enjoys the exclusive right to remove the [Scottish Crown Jewels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Crown_Jewels "Scottish Crown Jewels") from the City of [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] He also regularly attends sittings in the [Court of Lord Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Lord_Lyon "Court of Lord Lyon") as a hereditary [assessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assessor_/(law/) "Assessor (law)"), sitting on the bench beside [Lord Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Lyon "Lord Lyon").

The [courtesy titles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtesy_titles_in_the_United_Kingdom "Courtesy titles in the United Kingdom") used by [heirs apparent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heirs_apparent "Heirs apparent") are "Marquess of Douglas and Clydesdale" (the eldest son of the duke) and "Earl of Angus" (the eldest son of a marquess of Douglas and Clydesdale). No duke has had a great-grandson in direct line to the titles, but it is likely that the latter would be styled "Lord Abernethy" (the Lordship of Abernethy and Jedburgh Forest being the most senior available title).

Before the dukes succeeded to the Marquessate of Douglas and its subsidiary titles, the heirs apparent were styled initially "[Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Arran_/(Scotland/) "Earl of Arran (Scotland)")" (which had previously been used as a courtesy title by the marquesses of Hamilton) and later "Marquess of Clydesdale" (the former style then being adopted for a grandson in direct line). The heir apparent to the Earldom of Lanark (before that title merged with the dukedom) was styled "Lord Polmont".

The duke of Hamilton and Brandon is one of only five British peers to hold more than one dukedom, the others being:

*   the [Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William,_Prince_of_Wales "William, Prince of Wales") (who is [Duke of Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Cornwall "Duke of Cornwall"), [Duke of Rothesay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Rothesay "Duke of Rothesay"), and [Duke of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Cambridge "Duke of Cambridge"));
*   the [Duke of Buccleuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Buccleuch "Duke of Buccleuch") and [Queensberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Queensberry "Duke of Queensberry");
*   the [Duke of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Argyll "Duke of Argyll") (who holds two Dukedoms of Argyll); and
*   the [Duke of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Richmond "Duke of Richmond"), [Lennox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Lennox "Duke of Lennox") and [Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Gordon "Duke of Gordon")

Historically, several other peers have held multiple dukedoms, including the [Duke of Newcastle upon Tyne and Newcastle-under-Lyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Pelham-Holles,_1st_Duke_of_Newcastle "Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle"), the [Duke of Argyll and Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Campbell,_2nd_Duke_of_Argyll "John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll"), the [Duke of Monmouth and Buccleuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Scott,_1st_Duke_of_Monmouth "James Scott, 1st Duke of Monmouth") and the two [Dukes of Queensberry and Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Queensberry "Duke of Queensberry") and some other mainly royal dukes.

Gilbert de Hameldun is recorded as witnessing a charter confirming the gift of the church at Cragyn to the [Abbey of Paisley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paisley_Abbey "Paisley Abbey") in 1271. His ancestry is uncertain but he may have been the son of William de Hamilton (third son of [Robert de Beaumont, 3rd Earl of Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_de_Beaumont,_3rd_Earl_of_Leicester "Robert de Beaumont, 3rd Earl of Leicester")) and Mary of Strathearn. Gilbert de Hameldun married Isabella Randolph, daughter of [Thomas Randolph of Strathdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Randolph_of_Strathdon&action=edit&redlink=1 "Thomas Randolph of Strathdon (page does not exist)"), [Chamberlain of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamberlain_of_Scotland "Chamberlain of Scotland"). His heir was [Walter fitz Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_fitz_Gilbert_of_Cadzow "Walter fitz Gilbert of Cadzow"). He was governor of [Bothwell Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bothwell_Castle "Bothwell Castle") for the English Crown during the [First War of Scottish Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_War_of_Scottish_Independence "First War of Scottish Independence"). Following the [Battle of Bannockburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bannockburn "Battle of Bannockburn") in 1314, he gave refuge to the [Earl of Hertford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Hertford "Earl of Hertford") and other escapees, only to deliver them and Bothwell up to [Edward Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Bruce "Edward Bruce"). He then became a Bruce partisan. Sometime between 1315 and 1329, [Robert the Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_the_Bruce "Robert the Bruce") knighted him and granted him lands in [Renfrewshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renfrewshire "Renfrewshire") and the [Lothians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothian "Lothian") and Cadzow (present day [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_South_Lanarkshire "Hamilton, South Lanarkshire") in [Lanarkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanarkshire "Lanarkshire")), including [Cadzow Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadzow_Castle "Cadzow Castle"). The lands had previously belonged to [John Comyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III_Comyn "John III Comyn"), who was murdered by Robert the Bruce.

Undifferenced arms of the chief of Hamilton until 1503

The 1st laird of Cadzow was succeeded as the 2nd laird by his son [Sir David fitz Walter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_fitz_Walter_of_Cadzow "David fitz Walter of Cadzow"). He was a supporter of [King David II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_II_of_Scotland "David II of Scotland") and fought at the [Battle of Neville's Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Neville%27s_Cross "Battle of Neville's Cross") (Battle of Durham) where he was captured along with the King. His son [David Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hamilton_of_Cadzow "David Hamilton of Cadzow"), the 3rd laird, was the first to establish Hamilton as the family name. David Hamilton's son [Sir John Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hamilton_of_Cadzow "John Hamilton of Cadzow") became the 4th laird and was, in turn, succeeded as the 5th laird by his son [James Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton_of_Cadzow "James Hamilton of Cadzow").

### Lords Hamilton and Earls of Arran

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Lords Hamilton and Earls of Arran")\]

The 5th laird was succeeded as 6th laird by his son, [Sir James Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Lord_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Lord Hamilton"), who was created a [Lord of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_of_Parliament "Lord of Parliament") as **Lord Hamilton** on 3 July 1445.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-7) In early 1474, he married [Princess Mary, Countess of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Stewart,_Countess_of_Arran "Mary Stewart, Countess of Arran"), daughter of [King James II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_Scotland "James II of Scotland") and widow of [Thomas Boyd, 1st Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Boyd,_1st_Earl_of_Arran "Thomas Boyd, 1st Earl of Arran"). He was succeeded by his only legitimate son, [James, 2nd Lord Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Earl_of_Arran "James Hamilton, 1st Earl of Arran"). In 1490, then aged 15, he married the 13-year-old Elizabeth, Lady Hay, daughter of [Alexander Home, 2nd Lord Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Home,_2nd_Lord_Home "Alexander Home, 2nd Lord Home") and widow of Sir Thomas Hay, Master of Yester, son and heir of [John Hay, 1st Lord Hay of Yester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hay,_1st_Lord_Hay_of_Yester "John Hay, 1st Lord Hay of Yester"). However, it was later discovered that Sir Thomas Hay was still alive and the marriage was annulled. The 2nd Lord married secondly Janet, Lady Livingstone, daughter of Sir David Beaton of Creich and widow of Sir Robert Livingstone of Easter Wemyss and Drumry. He became a [Privy Counsellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_Scotland "Privy Council of Scotland") to [King James IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_IV "King James IV"), and helped to arrange his marriage to [Margaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Tudor "Margaret Tudor"), daughter of [King Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). As a reward, he was created **Earl of Arran** on 8 August 1503.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-8) He was succeeded by his elder son from his second marriage, [James, 2nd Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_Duke_of_Ch%C3%A2tellerault "James Hamilton, Duke of Châtellerault"). He was Regent of Scotland between 1542 and 1554, and guardian of the young [Mary, Queen of Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_Queen_of_Scots "Mary, Queen of Scots"). He was created [Duc de Châtellerault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duc_de_Ch%C3%A2tellerault "Duc de Châtellerault") in the [Peerage of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peerage_of_France "Peerage of France") in 1548 for his part in arranging the marriage of Queen Mary to [Francis, Dauphin of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II_of_France "Francis II of France"). This French Dukedom was forfeited when he switched allegiances in 1559. [Emperor Napoleon III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Napoleon_III "Emperor Napoleon III") "confirmed" this title for the [12th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton_Douglas,_12th_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton Douglas, 12th Duke of Hamilton") in the 19th century, but although the 12th Duke was heir male of the 2nd Earl, the legal effect of this "confirmation" is doubtful.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-9)

The 2nd Earl was succeeded by his eldest son, [James, 3rd Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_3rd_Earl_of_Arran "James Hamilton, 3rd Earl of Arran"), who had been proposed as a husband to Queen [Elizabeth I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England "Elizabeth I of England") in 1561. In 1562 he was declared insane, and in 1581 he resigned the Earldom to [James Stewart of Bothwellhaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stuart,_Earl_of_Arran "James Stuart, Earl of Arran"). However, in 1586 his resignation was ruled by the [Court of Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Session "Court of Session") to be the act of a madman and his honours were restored.

### Marquesses and Dukes of Hamilton

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Marquesses and Dukes of Hamilton")\]

The 3rd Earl's younger brother [John Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hamilton,_1st_Marquess_of_Hamilton "John Hamilton, 1st Marquess of Hamilton") (who was styled Lord Hamilton as is traditional for the younger sons of Earls[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-10)) was appointed to administer his brother's estates. He was created **Marquess of Hamilton**, **Earl of Arran** and **Lord Aven** on 17 April 1599.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-11) His son, [James, 2nd Marquess of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_2nd_Marquess_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 2nd Marquess of Hamilton") (who had been created **Lord Aberbrothwick** (or **Arbroath**) on 5 May 1608,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-12) before he succeeded) moved to England with [King James VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_I_of_England "James I of England"), and invested into the [Somers Isles Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somers_Isles_Company "Somers Isles Company"), an offshoot of the [Virginia Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Company "London Company"), buying the shares of [Lucy Russell, Countess of Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Russell,_Countess_of_Bedford "Lucy Russell, Countess of Bedford"). The Parish of [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Parish,_Bermuda "Hamilton Parish, Bermuda") in the Somers Isles (now [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda")) is named for him. Upon the death of his uncle in 1609 he succeeded as 4th Earl of Arran (of the 1503 creation) and 5th Lord Hamilton. He was also created **Earl of Cambridge** and **Baron Innerdale** in the [Peerage of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peerage_of_England "Peerage of England") on 16 June 1619.

His son, [James, 3rd Marquess of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton"), was created **Duke of Hamilton**, **Marquess of Clydesdale**, **Earl of Arran and Cambridge** and **Lord Aven and Innerdale** on 12 April 1643,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-13) with a special remainder allowing succession through the female line should his and his brother's heirs male fail. His son, Charles, Earl of Arran, died young and the 1st Duke's titles passed to his younger brother, [William, 2nd Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton"), who had already been created **Earl of Lanark** and **Lord Machanshire and Polmont** on 31 March 1639. A surrender and regrant in 1650 allowed these also to be inherited by the 1st Duke's elder daughter. Upon his death in 1651, with no further heirs in the immediate male line, the Dukedom (and the titles created with it), as well as the Earldom of Lanark (and the title created with it), passed to that daughter, [Anne, 3rd Duchess of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Hamilton,_3rd_Duchess_of_Hamilton "Anne Hamilton, 3rd Duchess of Hamilton"). The 1503 Earldom of Arran and the Lordship of Hamilton became dormant,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-14) and all the other titles (the Marquessate of Hamilton, the 1599 Earldom of Arran and the Lordships of Hamilton, Aven and Aberbrothwick in the Peerage of Scotland, and the Earldom of Cambridge and the Barony of Innerdale in the Peerage of England) became extinct.

In 1656, the 3rd Duchess married [William Douglas, 1st Earl of Selkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, Duke of Hamilton"), third son of [William Douglas, 1st Marquess of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Douglas,_1st_Marquess_of_Douglas "William Douglas, 1st Marquess of Douglas"). He had been created **Earl of Selkirk** and **Lord Daer and Shortcleuch** on 4 August 1646.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-Balfour_Paul_1907_381-15) He changed his surname to "Hamilton", and on 20 September 1660 was created **Duke of Hamilton**, **Marquess of Clydesdale**, **Earl of Arran, Lanark and Selkirk** and **Lord Aven, Machanshire, Polmont and Daer** [for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_peerage "Life peerage").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-Balfour_Paul_1907_381-15) In 1688, he resigned the Earldom of Selkirk and the Lordship of Daer and Shortcleuch, and those titles were regranted to his second son, with a special remainder designed to prevent them becoming merged with the Dukedom. (See [Earl of Selkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Selkirk "Earl of Selkirk") for the subsequent history of those titles, which were eventually inherited by the 12th Duke of Hamilton, becoming separated again from the Dukedom on the death of the 13th Duke in 1940).

On 9 July 1698, the 3rd Duchess resigned all her titles in favour of her eldest son, [James, Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_4th_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 4th Duke of Hamilton"), who thereby succeeded as 4th Duke in his mother's lifetime (his father had died in 1694). During the lead-up to the [Acts of Union 1707](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707 "Acts of Union 1707"), the 4th Duke was the leader of the anti-union party. He was created **Duke of Brandon**, in the [County of Suffolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffolk "Suffolk"), and **Baron Dutton**, in the [County of Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"), in the [Peerage of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peerage_of_Great_Britain "Peerage of Great Britain") on 10 September 1711,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-16) but was wrongfully refused a summons to the [Parliament of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Great_Britain "Parliament of Great Britain") under that title (although he continued to sit as a [Scottish representative peer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Scottish_representative_peers "List of Scottish representative peers")). He was killed in [a celebrated duel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton%E2%80%93Mohun_duel "Hamilton–Mohun duel") with [Charles Mohun, 4th Baron Mohun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mohun,_4th_Baron_Mohun "Charles Mohun, 4th Baron Mohun") (who also died) in [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") in London on 15 November 1712.

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Hamiltonpalacemorris_edited.jpg/330px-Hamiltonpalacemorris_edited.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hamiltonpalacemorris_edited.jpg)

[Hamilton Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Palace "Hamilton Palace"), the former family seat in [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_South_Lanarkshire "Hamilton, South Lanarkshire"), circa 1880.

The 4th Duke's son [James, 5th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_5th_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 5th Duke of Hamilton") was succeeded by his son [James, 6th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_6th_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 6th Duke of Hamilton"), and he by his son [James, 7th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_7th_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 7th Duke of Hamilton"). In 1761, the 7th Duke's second cousin twice removed, [Archibald Douglas, 1st Duke of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Douglas,_1st_Duke_of_Douglas "Archibald Douglas, 1st Duke of Douglas"), died without an heir. As the Duke of Hamilton, though still using the surname "Hamilton", was patrilineally a "Douglas" (through the 3rd Duchess's husband), the 7th Duke became heir male of the [House of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Douglas "House of Douglas") and inherited the Duke of Douglas's subsidiary titles (although not the Dukedom), succeeding as 4th Marquess of Douglas, 14th and 4th Earl of Angus and 4th Lord Abernethy and Jedburgh Forest. He died without issue and was succeeded by his brother [Douglas, 8th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Hamilton,_8th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Douglas Hamilton, 8th Duke of Hamilton"). He left no sons and the title passed back to his uncle, the 6th Duke's brother, [Archibald, 9th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Hamilton,_9th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Archibald Hamilton, 9th Duke of Hamilton"). He was succeeded by his son [Alexander, 10th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton,_10th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton, 10th Duke of Hamilton"), and then by his son [William, 11th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_11th_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 11th Duke of Hamilton"). The 11th Duke's son [William, 12th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton_Douglas,_12th_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton Douglas, 12th Duke of Hamilton") (who changed his surname to "Hamilton Douglas"), died without a male heir, and the Dukedom passed to his fourth cousin [Alfred, 13th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Douglas-Hamilton,_13th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Alfred Douglas-Hamilton, 13th Duke of Hamilton"),[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHesilrige1921435-17) who was descended from the 4th Duke of Hamilton and whose line of the family had adopted the surname "Douglas-Hamilton". His son was [Douglas, 14th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Douglas-Hamilton,_14th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Douglas Douglas-Hamilton, 14th Duke of Hamilton"), who was succeeded by his son [Angus, 15th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_Douglas-Hamilton,_15th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Angus Douglas-Hamilton, 15th Duke of Hamilton"). He died in 2010, and was succeeded by his son, the current Duke, [Alexander, 16th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Douglas-Hamilton,_16th_Duke_of_Hamilton "Alexander Douglas-Hamilton, 16th Duke of Hamilton").

### Succession to the Dukedom of Hamilton

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Succession to the Dukedom of Hamilton")\]

The letters patent that created the Dukedom of Hamilton contained a special remainder. It stipulated that the Dukedom should descend to:

1.  [heirs male](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heirs_male "Heirs male") [of the body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heirs_of_the_body "Heirs of the body") of the [grantee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton"), failing which to
2.  the grantee's [brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton") and heirs male of the body of the grantee's brother, failing which to
3.  the grantee's [eldest daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Hamilton,_3rd_Duchess_of_Hamilton "Anne Hamilton, 3rd Duchess of Hamilton") and heirs male of her body, failing which to
4.  nearest heirs whatsoever of the grantee.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-books.google.com-1)

As the first Duke and his brother (the second Duke) both died without surviving sons, the succession has, since 1651, been governed by the third rule given, with the dukedom going to the grantee's daughter (the third Duchess) and her heirs male.

George Douglas, an illegitimate son of [William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Douglas,_1st_Earl_of_Douglas "William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas"), was created **Earl of Angus** on 9 April 1389.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-18)

His descendant, [William, 11th Earl of Angus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Douglas,_1st_Marquess_of_Douglas "William Douglas, 1st Marquess of Douglas"), was created **Marquess of Douglas**, **Earl of Angus** and **Lord Abernethy and Jedburgh Forest** on 14 June 1633.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-19)

His great-grandson, [Archibald, 3rd Marquess of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Douglas,_1st_Duke_of_Douglas "Archibald Douglas, 1st Duke of Douglas"), was created **Duke of Douglas**, **Marquess of Angus and Abernethy**, **Viscount of Jedburgh Forest** and **Lord Douglas of Bonkill, Prestoun and Robertoun** on 10 April 1703.

He died, married but childless, in 1761, at which point the Dukedom of Douglas (and the titles created with it) became extinct, but the Marquessate of Douglas, both Earldoms of Angus and the Lordship of Abernethy and Jedburgh Forest passed to his second cousin twice removed and heir male, [James Hamilton, 7th Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_7th_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 7th Duke of Hamilton").

The achievement has two [crests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crest_/(heraldry/) "Crest (heraldry)"), namely: _1st, on a Ducal Coronet an Oak Tree rutted and penetrated transversely in the main stem by a Frame Saw proper the frame Or (for Hamilton); 2nd, on a Chapeau Gules turned up Ermine a Salamander in flames proper (for Douglas)_. The [supporters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supporters_/(heraldry/) "Supporters (heraldry)") are: _on either side an Antelope Argent armed unguled ducally gorged and chained Or_. Each crest has a [motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_heraldry "Scottish heraldry"), namely "_Through_" (over the 1st crest) and "_Jamais Arriere_" ("_Never Behind_") (over the 2nd crest).

This article is about the branch of Reformed Protestantism. For the method of church organization, see [Presbyterian polity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity").

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Fourth_Chicago.jpg/250px-Fourth_Chicago.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fourth_Chicago.jpg)

Sanctuary of [Fourth Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Presbyterian_Church_/(Chicago/) "Fourth Presbyterian Church (Chicago)") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), Illinois, U.S.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/First_Presbyterian_Church_of_Pittsburgh.png/250px-First_Presbyterian_Church_of_Pittsburgh.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Presbyterian_Church_of_Pittsburgh.png)

[First Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Presbyterian_Church_/(Pittsburgh/) "First Presbyterian Church (Pittsburgh)") in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh")

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Presbyterian-Church-in-Ireland-Logo.svg/250px-Presbyterian-Church-in-Ireland-Logo.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Presbyterian-Church-in-Ireland-Logo.svg)

The [burning bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_bush "Burning bush"), a common symbol used by Presbyterian churches, used by the [Presbyterian Church in Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Ireland "Presbyterian Church in Ireland").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-1) The [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") inscription underneath translates as "burning but flourishing". Alternative versions of the motto are also used, such as "Nec Tamen Consumebatur" (yet not consumed).

**Presbyterianism** ([_pres-bə-TE\-ree-a-nizm_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is a historically [Reformed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Christianity "Reformed Christianity") [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") tradition named after its form of [church government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_polity "Ecclesiastical polity") by representative assemblies of [elders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity#Elder "Presbyterian polity"), known as "presbyters".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-2) Though other Reformed churches are structurally similar, the word _Presbyterian_ is applied to churches that trace their roots to the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland") or to [English Dissenter groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Dissenters "English Dissenters") that were formed during the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), 1642 to 1651.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-3)

Presbyterian theology typically emphasises the [sovereignty of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty_of_God "Sovereignty of God"), the [authority of the Scriptures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_scriptura "Sola scriptura"), and the necessity of [grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_in_Christianity "Grace in Christianity") through [faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_in_Christianity "Faith in Christianity") in Christ. Scotland ensured Presbyterian church government in the 1707 [Acts of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707 "Acts of Union 1707"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-4) which created the [Kingdom of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain"). In fact, most Presbyterians in England have a Scottish connection. The Presbyterian denomination was also taken to [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), mostly by [Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Americans "Scottish Americans") and [Scots-Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotch-Irish_American "Scotch-Irish American") immigrants.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-5) Scotland's Presbyterian denominations hold to the [Reformed theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_theology "Reformed theology") of [John Calvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin "John Calvin") and his immediate successors, although there is a range of theological views within contemporary Presbyterianism. Local congregations of churches that use [Presbyterian polity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity") are governed by [sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_/(Presbyterianism/) "Session (Presbyterianism)") made up of representatives of the congregation ([elders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_elder "Presbyterian elder")), a [conciliar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conciliarity "Conciliarity") approach as with other levels of decision-making ([presbytery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbytery_/(church_polity/) "Presbytery (church polity)"), [synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_synod "Presbyterian synod"), and [general assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Assembly_/(presbyterian_church/) "General Assembly (presbyterian church)")). There are roughly 75 million Presbyterians in the world.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-6)

Presbyterianism's roots lie in the [Magisterial Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magisterial_Reformation "Magisterial Reformation") of the 16th century. John Calvin's [Republic of Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Geneva "Republic of Geneva") was particularly influential, along with Calvin's student, [Scottish Reformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Reformation "Scottish Reformation") [John Knox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Knox "John Knox") who worked with civil magistrates to establish the Presbyterian Church in Scotland, writing the book of [common order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Common_Order "Book of Common Order") and eventually the [Scots Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots_Confession "Scots Confession").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-7) Most Reformed churches that trace their history to Scotland are either presbyterian or [congregationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_polity "Congregational polity") in government. In the 20th century, some Presbyterians played an important role in the [ecumenical movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenism "Ecumenism"), including the [World Council of Churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Council_of_Churches "World Council of Churches"). Many Presbyterian denominations have found ways of working together with other Reformed denominations and Christians of other traditions, especially in the [World Communion of Reformed Churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Communion_of_Reformed_Churches "World Communion of Reformed Churches"). Some Presbyterian churches have entered into [unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_and_uniting_churches "United and uniting churches") with other churches, such as the [Continental Reformed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Reformed_Protestantism "Continental Reformed Protestantism"), [Congregationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_church "Congregational church"), [Lutherans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism"), [Anglicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism"), and [Methodists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodists "Methodists"). Presbyterians in the United States came largely from [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_American "Scottish American"), [Scots-Irish immigrants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotch-Irish_American "Scotch-Irish American"), and also from [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England") communities that were originally [Congregational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregationalism_in_the_United_States "Congregationalism in the United States") but changed because of an agreed-upon [Plan of Union of 1801](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_of_Union_of_1801 "Plan of Union of 1801") for frontier areas.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-8)

Presbyterian identity
---------------------

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/John_Knox_woodcut.jpg/250px-John_Knox_woodcut.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Knox_woodcut.jpg)

Presbyterian history is part of the [history of Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Christianity "History of Christianity"), but the beginning of Presbyterianism as a distinct movement occurred during the 16th century [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation"). As the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") resisted the Reformers, several different theological movements splintered from the Church and bore different denominations. The Presbyterian Church (The Church of Scotland) was a direct break off of the Roman Catholic Church as were the Anglican Church and the Lutheran Church.

Presbyterianism was especially influenced by the French theologian [John Calvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin "John Calvin"), who is credited with the development of [Reformed theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_theology "Reformed theology"), and the work of [John Knox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Knox "John Knox"), a Scottish Catholic Priest who studied with Calvin in Geneva and brought back Reformed teachings to Scotland. An important influence on the formation of Presbyterianism in Britain also came from [John a Lasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_%C5%81aski "Jan Łaski"), a Polish reformer, the founder of a [Stranger's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stranger_churches "Stranger churches") in London, based on the Geneva models.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-21)

The Presbyterian church traces its ancestry primarily to Scotland. In August 1560, the [Parliament of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland") adopted the [Scots Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots_Confession "Scots Confession") as the creed of the Scottish Kingdom. In December 1560, the _[First Book of Discipline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Book_of_Discipline "First Book of Discipline")_ was published, outlining important doctrinal issues but also establishing regulations for church government, including the creation of ten ecclesiastical districts with appointed superintendents which later became known as [presbyteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbytery_/(church_polity/) "Presbytery (church polity)").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-22)

In time, the Scots Confession would be supplanted by the [Westminster Confession of Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Confession_of_Faith "Westminster Confession of Faith"), and the [larger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Larger_Catechism "Westminster Larger Catechism") and [shorter catechisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism"), which were formulated by the [Westminster Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") between 1643 and 1649.

Presbyterians distinguish themselves from other denominations by [doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctrine "Doctrine"), institutional organisation (or "church order") and [worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worship "Worship"), often using a "Book of Order" to regulate common practice and order. The origins of the Presbyterian churches are in [Reformed Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Christianity "Reformed Christianity"), also called Calvinism. Many branches of Presbyterianism are remnants of previous splits from larger groups. Some of the splits have been due to doctrinal controversy, while some have been caused by disagreement concerning the degree to which those ordained to church office should be required to agree with the [Westminster Confession of Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Confession_of_Faith "Westminster Confession of Faith"), which historically serves as an important confessional document — second only to the Bible, yet directing particularities in the standardisation and translation of the Bible — in Presbyterian churches.

Presbyterians place importance on education and lifelong learning, tempered with the belief that no human action can affect [salvation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvation_in_Christianity "Salvation in Christianity").

Continuous study of the scriptures, theological writings, and understanding and interpretation of church doctrine are embodied in several statements of faith and [catechisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechism "Catechism") formally adopted by various branches of the church, often referred to as "[subordinate standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subordinate_standard "Subordinate standard")".

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Lorimer%2C_Ordination.jpg/250px-Lorimer%2C_Ordination.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lorimer,_Ordination.jpg)

Painting by [John Henry Lorimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henry_Lorimer "John Henry Lorimer"), _The Ordination of Elders in a Scottish Kirk_, 1891, now in the [National Gallery of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Scotland "National Gallery of Scotland")

Presbyterian government is by councils (still known as _courts_ in some countries, as _boards_ in others) of elders. Teaching and ruling elders are ordained and convene in the lowest council known as a [_session_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_/(Presbyterianism/) "Session (Presbyterianism)") or _[consistory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consistory_/(Protestantism/)#Reformed_usage "Consistory (Protestantism)")_ responsible for the discipline, nurture, and mission of the local [congregation](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/congregation "wiktionary:congregation"). Teaching elders (pastors or ministers) have responsibility for teaching, worship, and performing sacraments. Pastors or ministers are called by individual congregations. A congregation issues a call for the pastor or minister's service, but this call must be ratified by the local presbytery. The pastor or minister is a teaching elder, and Moderator of the Session, but is not usually a member of the congregation; instead, this person is a member of the Presbytery of which the given church is a member.

Ruling elders are elected by the congregation and ordained to serve with the teaching elders, assuming responsibility for the nurture and leadership of the congregation. Often, especially in larger congregations, the elders delegate the practicalities of buildings, finance, and temporal ministry to the needy in the congregation to a distinct group of officers (sometimes called deacons, which are ordained in some denominations). This group may variously be known as a "Deacon Board", "Board of Deacons" "Diaconate", or "Deacons' Court". These are sometimes known as "presbyters" to the full congregation. Since the 20th century, most denominations allow women to be teaching or ruling elders.

Above the sessions exist presbyteries, which have area responsibilities. These are composed of teaching elders and ruling elders from each of the constituent congregations. The presbytery sends representatives to a broader regional or national assembly, generally known as the [General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Assembly_/(presbyterian_church/) "General Assembly (presbyterian church)"), although an intermediate level of a _[synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod "Synod")_ sometimes exists. This congregation / [presbytery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbytery_/(presbyterian_church/) "Presbytery (presbyterian church)") / [synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod "Synod") / [general assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Assembly_/(presbyterian_church/) "General Assembly (presbyterian church)") schema is based on the historical structure of the larger Presbyterian churches, such as the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland") or the [Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_/(U.S.A./) "Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)"); some bodies, such as the [Presbyterian Church in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_America "Presbyterian Church in America") and the [Presbyterian Church in Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Ireland "Presbyterian Church in Ireland"), skip one of the steps between congregation and General Assembly, and usually the step skipped is the Synod. The [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland") abolished the Synod in 1993.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-23)

Presbyterian governance is practiced by Presbyterian denominations and also by many other [Reformed churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_churches "Reformed churches").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-24)

Presbyterianism is historically a confessional tradition. Confessional churches express their faith in the form of "confessions of faith", which have some level of authoritative status. In confessional churches, theology is not solely an individual matter. While individuals are encouraged to understand Scripture, and may challenge the current institutional understanding, theology is carried out by the community as a whole. It is this community understanding of theology that is expressed in confessions.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-lostsoul-26)

There is a spectrum of approaches to [confessionalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessionalism_/(religion/) "Confessionalism (religion)"). The manner of [subscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessional_subscription "Confessional subscription"), or the degree to which the official standards establish the actual doctrine of the church, is a practical matter leading to the decisions rendered in ordination and in the courts of the church to largely determine what the church means, representing the whole, by its adherence to the doctrinal standard.

Some Presbyterian traditions adopt only the [Westminster Confession of Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Confession_of_Faith "Westminster Confession of Faith") as the doctrinal standard to which teaching elders are required to subscribe, in contrast to the [Larger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Larger_Catechism "Westminster Larger Catechism") and [Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") catechisms, which are approved for use in instruction. Many Presbyterian denominations, especially in North America, have adopted all of the [Westminster Standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Standards "Westminster Standards") as their standard of doctrine which is subordinate to the Bible. These documents are [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinist "Calvinist") in their doctrinal orientation. The [Presbyterian Church in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Canada "Presbyterian Church in Canada") retains the Westminster Confession of Faith in its original form, while admitting the historical period in which it was written should be understood when it is read.

The Westminster Confession is "The principal [subordinate standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subordinate_standard "Subordinate standard") of the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland")" but "with due regard to liberty of opinion in points which do not enter into the substance of the Faith" (V).[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-27) This formulation represents many years of struggle over the extent to which the confession reflects the Word of God and the struggle of conscience of those who came to believe it did not fully do so (e.g. [William Robertson Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Robertson_Smith "William Robertson Smith")). Some Presbyterian churches, such as the [Free Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Church_of_Scotland_/(post_1900/) "Free Church of Scotland (post 1900)"), have no such "[conscience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscience "Conscience") clause".

The [Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_/(U.S.A./) "Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)") has adopted the _[Book of Confessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Confessions "Book of Confessions")_, which reflects the inclusion of other [Reformed confessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_confessions "Reformed confessions") in addition to the Westminster Standards. These other documents include ancient creedal statements (the [Nicene Creed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicene_Creed "Nicene Creed"), the [Apostles' Creed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostles%27_Creed "Apostles' Creed")), 16th-century Reformed confessions (the [Scots Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots_Confession "Scots Confession"), the [Heidelberg Catechism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidelberg_Catechism "Heidelberg Catechism"), the [Second Helvetic Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Helvetic_Confession "Second Helvetic Confession")), and 20th century documents ([The Theological Declaration of Barmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barmen_Declaration "Barmen Declaration"), [Confession of 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confession_of_1967 "Confession of 1967") and [A Brief Statement of Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Brief_Statement_of_Faith "A Brief Statement of Faith")).

The Presbyterian Church in Canada developed the confessional document _Living Faith_ (1984) and retains it as a subordinate standard of the denomination. It is confessional in format, yet like the Westminster Confession, draws attention to original Bible text.

Presbyterians in Ireland who rejected Calvinism and the Westminster Confessions formed the [Non-subscribing Presbyterian Church of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-subscribing_Presbyterian_Church_of_Ireland "Non-subscribing Presbyterian Church of Ireland").

[John Gresham Machen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Gresham_Machen "J. Gresham Machen"), the prominent Presbyterian theologian and Professor of [New Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Testament "New Testament") at [Princeton Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_Seminary "Princeton Seminary") between 1906 and 1929, led a revolt against modernist doctrine in his _Christianity and Liberalism_ (1923) that critiqued theological modernism. He argued that modernism and liberal theology was a false religion, a pretender that cloaks itself in Christian language – "Liberalism". This religion, he claimed, is a marriage of naturalism, humanism, secularism, and sentimentalism all rolled into one.

### Worship and sacraments

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Presbyterianism&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Worship and sacraments")\]

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Presbyterian_Catechising.jpg/250px-Presbyterian_Catechising.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Presbyterian_Catechising.jpg)

Presbyterian [catechising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechesis "Catechesis") in the 19th century

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/A_Scottish_Sacrament.jpg/250px-A_Scottish_Sacrament.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_Scottish_Sacrament.jpg)

_A Scottish Sacrament_, a portrait by Henry John Dobson

Presbyterian denominations that trace their heritage to the British Isles usually organise their church services inspired by the principles in the [Directory of Public Worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directory_of_Public_Worship "Directory of Public Worship"), developed by the [Westminster Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in the 1640s. This directory documented [Reformed worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_worship "Reformed worship") practices and theology adopted and developed over the preceding century by British [Puritans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritan "Puritan"), initially guided by John Calvin and John Knox. It was enacted as law by the [Parliament of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland"), and became one of the foundational documents of Presbyterian church legislation elsewhere.

Historically, the driving principle in the development of the standards of Presbyterian worship is the [Regulative principle of worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulative_principle_of_worship "Regulative principle of worship"), which specifies that (in worship), what is not commanded is forbidden.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-28)

Over subsequent centuries, many Presbyterian churches modified these prescriptions by introducing hymnody, instrumental accompaniment, and ceremonial [vestments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestment "Vestment") into worship. However, there is not one fixed "Presbyterian" worship style. Although there are set services for the [Lord's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord%27s_Day "Lord's Day") in keeping with [first-day Sabbatarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-day_Sabbatarianism "First-day Sabbatarianism"),[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-Wigley1980-29) one can find a service to be evangelical and even revivalist in tone (especially in some conservative denominations), or strongly liturgical, approximating the practices of [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") or more of [Anglicanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism"),\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] or semi-formal, allowing for a balance of hymns, preaching, and congregational participation (favored by many American Presbyterians). Most Presbyterian churches follow the traditional liturgical year and observe the traditional holidays, holy seasons, such as [Advent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advent "Advent"), Christmas, [Ash Wednesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ash_Wednesday "Ash Wednesday"), [Holy Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Week "Holy Week"), Easter, [Pentecost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecost "Pentecost"), etc. They also make use of the appropriate [seasonal liturgical colors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgical_colours#Reformed_churches "Liturgical colours"), etc. Many incorporate ancient liturgical prayers and responses into the communion services and follow a daily, seasonal, and festival lectionary. Other Presbyterians, however, such as the [Reformed Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_churches "Reformed Presbyterian churches"), would practice [a cappella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_cappella "A cappella") [exclusive psalmody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclusive_psalmody "Exclusive psalmody"), as well as eschew the celebration of holy days.

Among the [paleo-orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleo-orthodoxy "Paleo-orthodoxy") and [emerging church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerging_church "Emerging church") movements in Protestant and evangelical churches, in which some Presbyterians are involved, clergy are moving away from the traditional black [Geneva gown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_gown "Geneva gown") to such vestments as the [alb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alb "Alb") and [chasuble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasuble "Chasuble"), but also [cassock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassock "Cassock") and [surplice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surplice "Surplice") (typically a full-length Old English style surplice which resembles the [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts") alb, an ungirdled liturgical tunic of the old [Gallican Rite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallican_Rite "Gallican Rite")), which some, particularly those identifying with the Liturgical Renewal Movement, hold to be more ancient and representative of a more ecumenical past.

Presbyterian Church Communion Table

Presbyterians traditionally have held the Worship position that there are only two [sacraments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacraments "Sacraments"):

*   [Baptism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism "Baptism"), in which they [baptize infants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infant_baptism "Infant baptism"), as well as unbaptized adults by the [Aspersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspersion "Aspersion") (sprinkling) or [Affusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affusion "Affusion") (pouring) method in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, rather than the [Immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism#Immersion "Baptism") method.
*   The [Lord's Supper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucharist "Eucharist") (also known as Communion), in which Presbyterians believe in the Real Presence of Christ (pneumatic presence) in the spiritual sense, in the bread and wine through the Holy Spirit, as opposed to being locally present as in [transubstantiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transubstantiation "Transubstantiation").

Some early Presbyterians, which were influenced by the puritan movement, were careful to distinguish between the "church", which referred to the _members_, and the "meeting house", which was the building in which the church met. (Quakers still insist upon this distinction.) Until the late 19th century, very few Presbyterians ever referred to their buildings as "churches". Presbyterians believed that meeting-houses (now called churches) are buildings to support the worship of God. The [decor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_decoration "Interior decoration") in some instances was austere so as not to detract from worship. Early Presbyterian meeting-houses were extremely plain. No stained glass, no elaborate furnishings, and no images were to be found in the meeting-house. The pulpit, often raised so as only to be accessible by a staircase, was the centerpiece of the building. But these were not the standard characteristics of the mainline Presbyterians. These were more of the wave of Presbyterians that were influenced by the Puritans.

In the late 19th century a gradual shift began to occur. Prosperous congregations built imposing churches, such as [Fourth Presbyterian Church of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Presbyterian_Church_of_Chicago "Fourth Presbyterian Church of Chicago"), [Brick Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_Presbyterian_Church_/(New_York_City/) "Brick Presbyterian Church (New York City)") in New York City, [Shadyside Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadyside_Presbyterian_Church "Shadyside Presbyterian Church") in Pennsylvania, St Stephen Presbyterian in Fort Worth, Texas, and many others.

While Presbyterian churches historically reflected prevailing architectural trends, the 20th century saw a greater embrace of modern architectural styles, particularly the [modernist movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_architecture "Modern architecture") characterized by clean lines, geometric shapes, and open floor plans.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-30) Prominent examples include [Coral Ridge Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Ridge_Presbyterian_Church "Coral Ridge Presbyterian Church") in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, with expansive, light-filled sanctuary and angular design elements. Similarly, the [National Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Presbyterian_Church "National Presbyterian Church") in Washington, D.C., features a striking facade clad in limestone and punctuated by large windows, alongside abstract stained-glass windows. Both of these were designed by famed architect [Harold E. Wagoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_E._Wagoner "Harold E. Wagoner").

Usually a Presbyterian church will not have statues of saints, nor the ornate altar more typical of a [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") church. Instead, there is a "communion table", usually on the same level as the congregation, and sometimes elevated similar to an altar, however surrounded by the chancel. There may be a rail between the communion table and the chancel behind it, which may contain a more decorative altar-type table, choir loft, or choir stalls, lectern and clergy area. The altar is called the communion table, and the altar area is called the chancel by Presbyterians. In Presbyterian, and in Reformed churches, there may be an altar cross, either on the communion table or on a table in the chancel. By using the "empty" cross, or cross of the Westminster/Celtic cross, Presbyterians emphasize the resurrection and that Christ is not continually dying, but died once and is alive for all eternity. Quite a few Presbyterian church buildings are decorated with a cross, that has a circle around the center, or Celtic cross. This not only emphasizes the resurrection, but also acknowledges historical aspects of Presbyterianism. A baptismal font will be located either at the entrance or near the chancel area. Presbyterian architecture generally makes significant use of symbolism. One may also find decorative and ornate stained glass windows depicting scenes from the Bible. Some Presbyterian churches will also have ornate statues of Christ or graven scenes from the Last Supper located behind the chancel. [St. Giles' Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Giles%27_Cathedral "St. Giles' Cathedral") in Scotland has a crucifix next to an ornate elevated communion table that hangs alongside. The image of Christ is more of a faint image, with a more modern design.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-31)

_Covenanters in a Glen_, a depiction of an illegal [conventicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventicle "Conventicle")

[John Knox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Knox "John Knox") (1505–1572), a [Scot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people") who had spent time studying under [Calvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin "John Calvin") in Geneva, returned to [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") and urged his countrymen to reform the Church in line with [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism") doctrines. After a period of religious convulsion and political conflict culminating in a victory for the [Protestant party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords_of_the_Congregation "Lords of the Congregation") at the [Siege of Leith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Leith "Siege of Leith") the authority of the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") was abolished in favour of [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Reformation "Scottish Reformation") by the legislation of the [Scottish Reformation Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Reformation_Parliament "Scottish Reformation Parliament") in 1560. The Church was eventually organised by [Andrew Melville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Melville "Andrew Melville") along Presbyterian lines to become the national [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"). [King James VI and I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_VI_and_I "King James VI and I") moved the Church of Scotland towards an episcopal form of government, and in 1637, James' successor, [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") and [William Laud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud"), the [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), attempted to force the Church of Scotland to use the [Book of Common Prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Common_Prayer "Book of Common Prayer"). What resulted was an armed insurrection, with many Scots signing the _[Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant")_. The [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter "Covenanter") would serve as the government of Scotland for nearly a decade, and would also send military support to the [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") during the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"). Following the restoration of the monarchy in 1660, [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), despite the initial support that he received from the Covenanters, reinstated an episcopal form of government on the church.

However, with the [Glorious Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution "Glorious Revolution") of 1688 the Church of Scotland was unequivocally recognised as a Presbyterian institution by the monarch due to Scottish Presbyterian support for the aforementioned revolution and the [Acts of Union 1707](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707 "Acts of Union 1707") between Scotland and England guaranteed the Church of Scotland's form of government. However, legislation by the [United Kingdom parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_parliament "United Kingdom parliament") allowing [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") led to splits in the Church. In 1733, a group of ministers [seceded from the Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Secession "First Secession") to form the Associate Presbytery, another group seceded in 1761 to form the [Relief Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relief_Church "Relief Church") and the [Disruption of 1843](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disruption_of_1843 "Disruption of 1843") led to the formation of the [Free Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Church_of_Scotland_/(1843-1900/) "Free Church of Scotland (1843-1900)"). Further splits took place, especially over theological issues, but most Presbyterians in Scotland were reunited by the 1929 union of the established Church of Scotland and the [United Free Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Free_Church_of_Scotland "United Free Church of Scotland").

There are today ten Presbyterian denominations in Scotland. These are, listed by number of congregations within Scotland: the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"), the [Free Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Church_of_Scotland_/(post_1900/) "Free Church of Scotland (post 1900)"), the [United Free Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Free_Church_of_Scotland "United Free Church of Scotland"), the [Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Presbyterian_Church_of_Scotland "Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland"), the [Free Church of Scotland (Continuing)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Church_of_Scotland_/(Continuing/) "Free Church of Scotland (Continuing)"), the [Didasko Presbytery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didasko "Didasko"),[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-32) the [Associated Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Presbyterian_Churches "Associated Presbyterian Churches"), the [Reformed Presbyterian Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_Church_of_Scotland "Reformed Presbyterian Church of Scotland"), the [International Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Presbyterian_Church "International Presbyterian Church") and two congregations of the [Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Presbyterian_Church_of_Ulster "Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster"). Combined, they have over 1500 congregations in Scotland.

Within Scotland the term "[kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_/(word/) "Kirk (word)")" is usually used to refer to a local Presbyterian church. Informally, the term "The Kirk" refers to the Church of Scotland. Some of the values and ideals espoused in Scottish Presbyterian denominations can be reflected in this reference in a book from Norman Drummond, chaplain to the Queen in Scotland.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-33)
