In England, Presbyterianism was established in secret in 1592. [Thomas Cartwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cartwright_/(Puritan/) "Thomas Cartwright (Puritan)") is thought to be the first Presbyterian in England. Cartwright's controversial lectures at [Cambridge University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University "Cambridge University") condemning the [episcopal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity") hierarchy of the [Elizabethan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_era "Elizabethan era") Church led to his deprivation of his post by Archbishop [John Whitgift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Whitgift "John Whitgift") and his emigration abroad. Between 1645 and 1648, a series of ordinances of the [Long Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament") established Presbyterianism as the polity of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"). Presbyterian government was established in London and Lancashire and in a few other places in England, although Presbyterian hostility to the [execution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Charles_I "Execution of Charles I") of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") and the establishment of the republican [Commonwealth of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") meant that Parliament never enforced the Presbyterian system in England. The [Restoration of the monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in 1660 brought the return of [Episcopal church government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity") in England (and in Scotland for a short time); but the Presbyterian church in England continued in Non-Conformity, outside of the established church. In 1719 a major split, the [Salter's Hall controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bradbury_/(minister/) "Thomas Bradbury (minister)"), occurred; with the majority siding with [nontrinitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nontrinitarian "Nontrinitarian") views. [Thomas Bradbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bradbury_/(minister/) "Thomas Bradbury (minister)") published several sermons bearing on the controversy, and in 1719, "An answer to the reproaches cast on the [dissenting ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissenting_minister "Dissenting minister") who subscribed their belief of the Eternal Trinity." By the 18th century many English Presbyterian congregations had become [Unitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitarianism "Unitarianism") in doctrine.

A number of new Presbyterian Churches were founded by [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people") immigrants to England in the 19th century and later. Following the 'Disruption' in 1843 many of those linked to the Church of Scotland eventually joined what became the [Presbyterian Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_England "Presbyterian Church of England") in 1876. Some, such as Crown Court (Covent Garden, London), St Andrew's (Stepney, London) and [Swallow Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swallow_Street "Swallow Street") (London), did not join the English denomination, which is why there are Church of Scotland congregations in England such as those at [Crown Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Court_Church "Crown Court Church"), and [St Columba's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Columba%27s_Church,_London "St Columba's Church, London"), Pont Street (Knightsbridge) in London. There is also a congregation in the heart of London's financial district called London City Presbyterian Church that is affiliated with the Free Church of Scotland.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-34) The Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland also have a congregation in London,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-35) as do the Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster – along with five others in England.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-36)

In 1972, the [Presbyterian Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_England "Presbyterian Church of England") (PCofE) united with the [Congregational Church in England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_Church_in_England_and_Wales "Congregational Church in England and Wales") to form the [United Reformed Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Reformed_Church "United Reformed Church") (URC). Among the congregations the PCofE brought to the URC were Tunley (Lancashire), [Aston Tirrold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Tirrold "Aston Tirrold") (Oxfordshire) and John Knox Presbyterian Church, Stepney, London (now part of [Stepney Meeting House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stepney_Meeting_House "Stepney Meeting House") URC) – these are among the sole survivors today of the English Presbyterian churches of the 17th century. The URC also has a presence in Scotland, mostly of former [Congregationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_church "Congregational church") Churches. Two former Presbyterian congregations, [St Columba's, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downing_Place_United_Reformed_Church,_Cambridge#St_Columba's_Church "Downing Place United Reformed Church, Cambridge") (founded in 1879), and [St Columba's, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Columba%27s_United_Reformed_Church,_Oxford "St Columba's United Reformed Church, Oxford") (founded as a chaplaincy by the PCofE and the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland") in 1908 and as a congregation of the PCofE in 1929), continue as congregations of the URC and university chaplaincies of the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland").

In recent years a number of smaller denominations adopting Presbyterian forms of church government have organised in England, including the [International Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Presbyterian_Church "International Presbyterian Church") planted by evangelical theologian [Francis Schaeffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Schaeffer "Francis Schaeffer") of the [L'Abri Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27Abri "L'Abri") in the 1970s – now with fifteen English-speaking congregations in England, and 6 Korean-speaking congregations. There is also the [Evangelical Presbyterian Church in England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Presbyterian_Church_in_England_and_Wales "Evangelical Presbyterian Church in England and Wales") founded in the North of England in the late 1980s.

In [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"), Presbyterianism is represented by the [Presbyterian Church of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_Wales "Presbyterian Church of Wales"), which was originally composed largely of [Calvinistic Methodists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinistic_Methodists "Calvinistic Methodists") who accepted Calvinist theology rather than the [Arminianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arminianism "Arminianism") of the Wesleyan Methodists. They broke off from the Church of England in 1811, ordaining their own ministers. They were originally known as the Calvinist Methodist connexion and in the 1920s it became alternatively known as the Presbyterian Church of Wales.

Presbyterianism ([Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_language "Irish language"): _Preispitéireachas_, [Ulster Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_Scots_dialect "Ulster Scots dialect"): _Prisbytairinism_) is the largest Protestant denomination in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") and the second largest on the island of Ireland (after the [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") [Church of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Ireland "Church of Ireland")),[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-37) and was brought by Scottish [plantation settlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantation_of_Ulster "Plantation of Ulster") to [Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster "Ulster") who had been strongly encouraged to emigrate by James VI of Scotland, also [James I of Ireland and England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_I_of_England "James I of England"). After the start of the plantation of Ulster in 1606, several thousand Scottish Presbyterians moved to the northern counties of Ireland.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-UHF-38) The first official [Presbyterian gathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Brice "Edward Brice") in Ireland was held in 1613.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-39) The Presbytery of Ulster was formed in 1642 separately from the established Anglican Church; by 1659 there were nearly 80 presbyteries.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-UHF-38) By 1715, the northern province of Ulster had a population of 600,000; more than 200,000 of these came from Scotland.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-40)

Presbyterians, along with [Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") in Ulster and the rest of Ireland, suffered under the discriminatory [Penal Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_Laws_against_Irish_Catholics "Penal Laws against Irish Catholics") until they were revoked in the early 19th century. Presbyterianism is represented in Ireland by the [Presbyterian Church in Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Ireland "Presbyterian Church in Ireland"), the [Non-subscribing Presbyterian Church of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-subscribing_Presbyterian_Church_of_Ireland "Non-subscribing Presbyterian Church of Ireland"), the [Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Presbyterian_Church_of_Ulster "Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster"), the [Reformed Presbyterian Church of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_Church_of_Ireland "Reformed Presbyterian Church of Ireland") and the [Evangelical Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Presbyterian_Church_/(Ireland/) "Evangelical Presbyterian Church (Ireland)").

There is a Church of Scotland (Presbyterian) in central Paris: [The Scots Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Scots_Kirk,_Paris "The Scots Kirk, Paris"), which is English-speaking, and is attended by many nationalities. It maintains close links with the Church of Scotland in Scotland itself, as well as with the [Reformed Church of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Church_of_France "Reformed Church of France").

The Waldensian Evangelical Church (Chiesa Evangelica Valdese, CEV) is an Italian Protestant denomination. The church was founded in the 12th century. After the Protestant Reformation, it adhered to Calvinist theology and became the Italian branch of the Presbyterian churches. As such, the church is a member of the World Communion of Reformed Churches.

Even before Presbyterianism spread with immigrants abroad from Scotland, there were divisions in the larger Presbyterian family. Some later rejoined only to separate again. In what some interpret as rueful self-reproach, some Presbyterians refer to the divided Presbyterian churches as the "Split Ps".

Presbyterianism first officially arrived in Colonial America in 1644 with the establishment of Christ's First Presbyterian Church in Heemstede/ Hempstead, Nieuw Amsterdam/ New York. The Church was organized by the Rev. Richard Denton.

In 1703 the first Presbytery in Philadelphia was established. In time, the presbytery would be joined by two more to form a synod (1717) and would evolve into the [Presbyterian Church in the United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_the_United_States_of_America "Presbyterian Church in the United States of America") in 1789. The nation's largest Presbyterian denomination, the [Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_/(U.S.A./) "Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)") – PC (USA) – can trace its heritage to the original PCUSA, as can the [Presbyterian Church in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_America "Presbyterian Church in America") (PCA), the [Orthodox Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Presbyterian_Church "Orthodox Presbyterian Church") (OPC), the [Bible Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_Presbyterian_Church "Bible Presbyterian Church") (BPC), the [Cumberland Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Presbyterian_Church "Cumberland Presbyterian Church") (CPC), the [Cumberland Presbyterian Church in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Presbyterian_Church_in_America "Cumberland Presbyterian Church in America"), the [Evangelical Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Presbyterian_Church_/(United_States/) "Evangelical Presbyterian Church (United States)") (EPC), and the [Evangelical Covenant Order of Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Covenant_Order_of_Presbyterians "Evangelical Covenant Order of Presbyterians") (ECO).

Other Presbyterian bodies in the United States include the [Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_Church_of_North_America "Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America") (RPCNA), the [Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_Reformed_Presbyterian_Church "Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church") (ARP), the [Reformed Presbyterian Church in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_Church_in_the_United_States "Reformed Presbyterian Church in the United States") (RPCUS), the [Reformed Presbyterian Church General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_Church_General_Assembly "Reformed Presbyterian Church General Assembly"), the [Reformed Presbyterian Church – Hanover Presbytery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_Church_%E2%80%93_Hanover_Presbytery "Reformed Presbyterian Church – Hanover Presbytery"), the [Covenant Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenant_Presbyterian_Church "Covenant Presbyterian Church"), the Presbyterian Reformed Church, the Westminster Presbyterian Church in the United States, the [Korean American Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_American_Presbyterian_Church "Korean American Presbyterian Church"), and the [Free Presbyterian Church of North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Presbyterian_Church_of_North_America "Free Presbyterian Church of North America").

The territory within about a 50-mile (80 km) radius of [Charlotte, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina"), is historically the greatest concentration of Presbyterianism in the Southern United States, while an almost identical geographic area around [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Pennsylvania, contains probably the largest number of Presbyterians in the nation.

The PC (USA), beginning with its predecessor bodies, has, in common with other so-called "mainline" Protestant denominations, experienced a significant decline in members in recent years. Some estimates have placed that loss at nearly half in the last forty years.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-41)

Presbyterian influence, especially through [Princeton theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_theology "Princeton theology"), can be traced in modern [Evangelicalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism "Evangelicalism"). [Randall Balmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall_Balmer "Randall Balmer") says that:

> Evangelicalism itself, I believe, is a quintessentially North American phenomenon, deriving as it did from the confluence of [Pietism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietism "Pietism"), Presbyterianism, and the vestiges of [Puritanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritanism "Puritanism"). Evangelicalism picked up the peculiar characteristics from each strain – warmhearted spirituality from the Pietists (for instance), doctrinal precisionism from the Presbyterians, and individualistic introspection from the Puritans – even as the North American context itself has profoundly shaped the various manifestations of evangelicalism: fundamentalism, neo-evangelicalism, the holiness movement, Pentecostalism, the charismatic movement, and various forms of African-American and Hispanic evangelicalism.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-42)

— Randall Balmer, The Encyclopedia of Evangelicalism (2002)

In the late 1800s, Presbyterian missionaries established a presence in what is now northern [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"). This provided an alternative to the Catholicism, which was brought to the area by the Spanish [Conquistadors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistador "Conquistador") and had remained unchanged. The area experienced a "mini" reformation, in that many converts were made to Presbyterianism, prompting persecution. In some cases, the converts left towns and villages to establish their own neighboring villages. The arrival of the United States to the area prompted the Catholic church to modernize and make efforts at winning the converts back, many of which did return. However, there are still stalwart Presbyterians and Presbyterian churches in the area.

Lutherans, [Episcopalians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_/(USA/) "Episcopal Church (USA)"), and Presbyterians historically tend to be considerably wealthier[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-THE_EPISCOPALIANS-43) and have been better educated (having more [graduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_degree "Academic degree") and post-graduate degrees per capita) than most other religious groups in United States.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-44)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-45) They are disproportionately represented in the upper reaches of American business,[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-46) law, and politics.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-47)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-48)\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] They are part of a group known as [White Anglo-Saxon Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Anglo-Saxon_Protestants "White Anglo-Saxon Protestants") (WASPs).

In Canada, the largest Presbyterian denomination – and the largest Protestant denomination – was the [Presbyterian Church in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Canada "Presbyterian Church in Canada"), formed in 1875 with the merger of four regional groups. In 1925, the [United Church of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Church_of_Canada "United Church of Canada") was formed by the majority of Presbyterians combining with the [Methodist Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist_Church_/(Canada/) "Methodist Church (Canada)") and the [Congregational Union of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_church "Congregational church"). A sizable minority of Canadian Presbyterians, primarily in southern [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") but also throughout the nation, withdrew, and reconstituted themselves as a non-concurring continuing Presbyterian body. They regained use of the original name in 1939.

Presbyterianism arrived in Latin America in the 19th century.

[National Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Presbyterian_Church_in_Mexico "National Presbyterian Church in Mexico") in the historic center of [San Luis Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Luis_Potos%C3%AD_/(city/) "San Luis Potosí (city)"), Mexico

The biggest Presbyterian church is the [National Presbyterian Church in Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Presbyterian_Church_in_Mexico "National Presbyterian Church in Mexico") (_Iglesia Nacional Presbiteriana de México_), which has around 2,500,000 members and associates and 3000 congregations, but there are other small denominations like the Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church in Mexico which was founded in 1875 by the Associate Reformed Church in North America. The [Independent Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Presbyterian_Church_in_Mexico "Independent Presbyterian Church in Mexico"), the Presbyterian Reformed Church in Mexico, and the [National Conservative Presbyterian Church in Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Conservative_Presbyterian_Church_in_Mexico "National Conservative Presbyterian Church in Mexico") are existing churches in the Reformed tradition.

In Brazil, the [Presbyterian Church of Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_Brazil "Presbyterian Church of Brazil") (_Igreja Presbiteriana do Brasil_) totals approximately 1,011,300 members;[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-49) other Presbyterian churches (Independents, United, Conservatives, Renovated, etc.) in this nation have around 350,000 members. The [Renewed Presbyterian Church in Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewed_Presbyterian_Church_in_Brazil "Renewed Presbyterian Church in Brazil") was influenced by the charismatic movement and has about 131 000 members as of 2011.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-50) The [Conservative Presbyterian Church in Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Presbyterian_Church_in_Brazil "Conservative Presbyterian Church in Brazil") was founded in 1940 and has eight presbyteries.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-51) The Fundamentalist Presbyterian church in Brazil was influenced by [Carl McIntire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_McIntire "Carl McIntire") and the US [Bible Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_Presbyterian_Church "Bible Presbyterian Church") and has around 1 800 members. The [Independent Presbyterian Church of Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Presbyterian_Church_of_Brazil "Independent Presbyterian Church of Brazil") was founded in 1903 by Rev. Eduardo Carlos Pereira, has 500 congregations and 75 000 members. The [United Presbyterian Church of Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Presbyterian_Church_of_Brazil "United Presbyterian Church of Brazil") has around 4 000 members. There are also ethnic Korean Presbyterian churches in the country. The [Evangelical Reformed Churches in Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Reformed_Churches_in_Brazil "Evangelical Reformed Churches in Brazil") has Dutch origin. The [Reformed Churches in Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Churches_in_Brazil "Reformed Churches in Brazil") were recently founded by the [Canadian Reformed Churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_and_American_Reformed_Churches "Canadian and American Reformed Churches") with the [Reformed Churches in the Netherlands (Liberated)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Churches_in_the_Netherlands_/(Liberated/) "Reformed Churches in the Netherlands (Liberated)").

[Congregational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_church "Congregational church") churches present in the country are also part of the Calvinistic tradition in Latin America.

#### Other Latin American states

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Presbyterianism&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Other Latin American states")\]

There are probably more than four million members of Presbyterian churches in all of Latin America. Presbyterian churches are also present in Peru, Bolivia, Cuba, Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela, Colombia, Chile, Paraguay, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Argentina, Honduras and others, but with few members. The Presbyterian Church in Belize has 17 churches and church plants and there is a Reformed Seminary founded in 2004. Some Latin Americans in North America are active in the [Presbyterian Cursillo Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Cursillo_Movement "Presbyterian Cursillo Movement").

[Christ Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Presbyterian_Church,_Akropong "Christ Presbyterian Church, Akropong") in [Akropong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akropong "Akropong"), Ghana

Presbyterianism arrived in Africa in the 19th century through the work of Scottish missionaries and founded churches such as [St Michael and All Angels Church, Blantyre, Malawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Michael_and_All_Angels_Church,_Blantyre,_Malawi "St Michael and All Angels Church, Blantyre, Malawi"). The church has grown extensively and now has a presence in at least 23 countries in the region.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-52)

African Presbyterian churches often incorporate diaconal ministries, including social services, emergency relief, and the operation of mission hospitals. A number of partnerships exist between presbyteries in Africa and the PC(USA), including specific connections with Lesotho, Cameroon, Malawi, South Africa, Ghana and Zambia. For example, the Lackawanna Presbytery, located in Northeastern Pennsylvania, has a partnership with a presbytery in Ghana. Also the Southminster Presbyterian Church, located near Pittsburgh, has partnerships with churches in Malawi and Kenya. The Presbyterian Church of Nigeria, western Africa is also active in mostly the southern states of this nation with strong density in the south-eastern states. [Hope Waddel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Masterton_Waddell "Hope Masterton Waddell")'s missionary expedition in the mid 19th century, and later [Mary Slessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Slessor "Mary Slessor")'s work in coastal regions of the then British colony has brought about the church in these areas.

**Cameroon**

The [Presbyterian Church in Cameroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Cameroon "Presbyterian Church in Cameroon") is a member of reformed churches in Cameroon.

The [Presbyterian Church of East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_East_Africa "Presbyterian Church of East Africa"), based in Kenya, has 500 clergy and 4 million members.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-53)

The Reformed Presbyterian Church in Malawi (RPCM) has 150 congregations and 17 000–20 000 members\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]. It was a mission of the Free Presbyterian church of Scotland. The Restored Reformed Church works with RPCM. Evangelical Presbyterian Church in Malawi is an existing small church. Part of the Presbyterian Church in Malawi and Zambia is known as CCAP, Church of Central Africa-Presbyterian. Often the churches there have one main congregation and a number of prayer houses. Education, health ministries, and worship and spiritual development are important.

The Bantu Presbyterian Church of South Africa was formed in 1923, following missionary work by the Free Church of Scotland with indigenous Africans at the Lovedale Mission.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-54) In 1992, it was renamed as the Reformed Presbyterian Church.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-55) In 1999, it united with the (historically European) Presbyterian Church in South Africa to form the [Uniting Presbyterian Church in Southern Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniting_Presbyterian_Church_in_Southern_Africa "Uniting Presbyterian Church in Southern Africa").[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-56)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-57)

*   [The Presbyterian Church of South Sudan and Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Sudan "Presbyterian Church in Sudan"), founded in 1902 by American missionaries in [Malakal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malakal "Malakal"), was deprived of foreign pastors since 1962 by decision of the Sudanese government but it continued to grow. It is now the 3rd largest Christian church in Sudan with 1,000,000 members, shared between [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan") and [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan").[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-PCSSS-58)
*   The [Presbyterian Evangelical Church of Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan_Evangelical_Presbyterian_Church "Sudan Evangelical Presbyterian Church") was founded in the north of the country and in Khartoum by the same American missionaries in the late 19th century but left under the guidance of Egyptian evangelical pastors of Coptic origin.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-PCSSS-58)

In addition, there are a number of Presbyterian Churches in north Africa, the most known is the Nile Synod in Egypt and a recently founded synod for Sudan.

[The Hong Kong Council of the Church of Christ in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hong_Kong_Council_of_the_Church_of_Christ_in_China "The Hong Kong Council of the Church of Christ in China") (CCC) is a uniting church formed by [Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterians "Presbyterians") and [Congregationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregationalists "Congregationalists"), which inherited the [Reformed tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_tradition "Reformed tradition"). [HKCCCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hong_Kong_Council_of_the_Church_of_Christ_in_China "The Hong Kong Council of the Church of Christ in China") is also the only [mainline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainline_Protestant "Mainline Protestant") Reformed church in Hong Kong.

[Cumberland Presbyterian Church Yao Dao Secondary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Presbyterian_Church_Yao_Dao_Secondary_School "Cumberland Presbyterian Church Yao Dao Secondary School") is a Presbyterian school in [Yuen Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuen_Long "Yuen Long"), [New Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Territories "New Territories"). The [Cumberland Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Presbyterian_Church "Cumberland Presbyterian Church") also have a church on the island of [Cheung Chau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheung_Chau "Cheung Chau"). There are also [Korean Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Christians_in_Hong_Kong "Korean Christians in Hong Kong") resident in Hong Kong who are Presbyterians.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-59)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-60)

Presbyterian Churches are the biggest and by far the most influential Protestant denominations in South Korea, with close to 20,000 churches affiliated with the two largest Presbyterian denominations in the country.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-61) In South Korea there are 9 million Presbyterians, forming the majority of the 15 million Korean [Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant"). In South Korea there are 100 different Presbyterian denominations.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-62)

Most of the Korean Presbyterian denominations share the same name in Korean, 대한예수교장로회 (literally means the Presbyterian Church of Korea or PCK), tracing its roots to the United Presbyterian Assembly. A Presbyterian schism began with a Japanese shrine worship enforced during the Japanese colonial period and the establishment of a minor division (Koryu-pa, 고려파, later The Koshin Presbyterian Church in Korea, Koshin 고신) in 1952. In 1953 a second schism happened when the theological orientation of the Chosun Seminary (later [Hanshin University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanshin_University "Hanshin University")) founded in 1947 could not be tolerated in the PCK and another minor group (The [Presbyterian Church in the Republic of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_the_Republic_of_Korea "Presbyterian Church in the Republic of Korea"), Kijang, 기장) was separated. The last major schism had to do with the issue of whether the PCK should join the WCC. The controversy divided the PCK into two denominations, The Presbyterian Church of Korea (Tonghap, 통합) and The General Assembly of Presbyterian Church in Korea (Hapdong, 합동) in 1959. All major seminaries associated with each denomination claim heritage from the [Pyung Yang Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang_Theological_Seminary "Pyongyang Theological Seminary").[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-63)

Korean Presbyterian denominations are active in evangelism and many of its missionaries are being sent overseas, being the second biggest missionary sender in the world after the United States. GMS, the missionary body of the "Hapdong" General Assembly of Presbyterian Churches of Korea, is the single largest Presbyterian missionary organization in Korea.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-64) In addition there are many Korean-American Presbyterians in the United States, either with their own church sites or sharing space in pre-existing churches as is the case in Australia, New Zealand and even Muslim countries such as Saudi Arabia with Korean immigration.

The Korean Presbyterian Church started through the mission of the Presbyterian Church (USA) and the Australian Presbyterian theological tradition is central to the United States. But after independence, the 'Presbyterian Church in Korea (KoRyuPa)' advocated a Dutch [Reformed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_tradition "Reformed tradition") position. In the 21st century, a new General Assembly of the Orthodox Presbyterian Church of Korea (Founder. [Ha Seung-moo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ha_Seung-moo "Ha Seung-moo")) in 2012 declared itself an authentic historical succession of Scottish Presbyterian John Knox.

The [Presbyterian Church in Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Taiwan "Presbyterian Church in Taiwan") (PCT) is by far the largest Protestant denomination in [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), with some 238,372 members as of 2009 (including a majority of the island's [aborigines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formosan_Aboriginals "Formosan Aboriginals")). [English Presbyterian Missionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Presbyterian_Mission "English Presbyterian Mission") [James Laidlaw Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Laidlaw_Maxwell "James Laidlaw Maxwell") established the first Presbyterian church in [Tainan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tainan "Tainan") in 1865. His colleague [George Leslie Mackay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Leslie_Mackay "George Leslie Mackay"), of the [Canadian Presbyterian Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Presbyterian_Mission "Canadian Presbyterian Mission"), was active in [Tamsui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamsui "Tamsui") and north Taiwan from 1872 to 1901; he founded the island's first university and hospital, and created a written script for [Taiwanese Minnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwanese_Minnan "Taiwanese Minnan"). The English and Canadian missions joined as the PCT in 1912. One of the few churches permitted to operate in Taiwan through the era of Japanese rule (1895–1945), the PCT experienced rapid growth during the era of [Kuomintang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuomintang "Kuomintang")\-imposed martial law (1949–1987), in part due to its support for democracy, human rights, and [Taiwan independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_independence "Taiwan independence"). Former [ROC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China") president [Lee Teng-hui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Teng-hui "Lee Teng-hui") (in office 1988–2000) was a Presbyterian.

Jowai Presbyterian Church in India

In the mainly Christian Indian state of [Mizoram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizoram "Mizoram"), Presbyterianism is the largest of all [Christian denominations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_denomination "Christian denomination"). It was brought there by [missionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionaries "Missionaries") from [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales") in 1897. Prior to Mizoram, Welsh Presbyterians started venturing into northeast India through the [Khasi Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khasi_Hills "Khasi Hills") (now in the state of [Meghalaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meghalaya "Meghalaya") in India) and established Presbyterian churches all over the Khasi Hills from the 1840s onwards. Hence, there is a strong presence of Presbyterians in [Shillong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shillong "Shillong") (the present capital of Meghalaya) and the areas adjoining it. The Welsh missionaries built their first church in [Sohra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sohra "Sohra") (aka [Cherrapunji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherrapunji "Cherrapunji")) in 1846. The Presbyterian church in India was integrated in 1970 into the [United Church of Northern India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Church_of_Northern_India_%E2%80%93_Presbyterian_Synod "United Church of Northern India – Presbyterian Synod") (originally formed in 1924). It is the largest Presbyterian denomination in India.

[![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Timeline_of_Aust._Pres._Denominations.png/500px-Timeline_of_Aust._Pres._Denominations.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Timeline_of_Aust._Pres._Denominations.png)

Timeline of the Presbyterian denominations in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") over the past century, and the movement of congregations from one to another

In [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), Presbyterianism is the fourth largest denomination of Christianity, with nearly 600,000 Australians claiming to be Presbyterian in the 2006 Commonwealth Census. Presbyterian churches were founded in each colony, some with links to the Church of Scotland and others to the Free Church. There were also congregations originating from United Presbyterian Church of Scotland as well as a number founded by [John Dunmore Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dunmore_Lang "John Dunmore Lang"). Most of these bodies merged between 1859 and 1870, and in 1901 formed a federal union called the [Presbyterian Church of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_Australia "Presbyterian Church of Australia") but retaining their state assemblies. The [Presbyterian Church of Eastern Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_Eastern_Australia "Presbyterian Church of Eastern Australia") representing the Free Church of Scotland tradition, and congregations in Victoria of the [Reformed Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Presbyterian_Church_of_Australia "Reformed Presbyterian Church of Australia"), originally from Ireland, are the other existing denominations dating from colonial times.

In 1977, about 70% of the Presbyterian Church of Australia, along with most of the [Congregational Union of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_Union_of_Australia "Congregational Union of Australia") and all the [Methodist Church of Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist_Church_of_Australasia "Methodist Church of Australasia"), combined to form the [Uniting Church in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniting_Church_in_Australia "Uniting Church in Australia").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-65) The 30% that did not unite had various reasons for so acting, often cultural attachment but often conservative theological or social views. The permission for the ordination of women given in 1974 was rescinded in 1991.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-Rev-66) This did not affect the two or three existing woman ministers.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The approval of women elders given in the 1960s has been rescinded in most states.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism#cite_note-Rev-66) The exception was New South Wales, which has the largest membership.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The theology of the church is now generally conservative and Reformed.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] A number of small Presbyterian denominations have arisen since the 1950s through migration or schism.

[Kaikorai Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaikorai_Presbyterian_Church "Kaikorai Presbyterian Church") in [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand")

In [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), Presbyterian is the dominant denomination in [Otago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otago "Otago") and [Southland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southland_Region "Southland Region") due largely to the rich [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people") and to a lesser extent [Ulster-Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_Scots_people "Ulster Scots people") heritage in the region. The area around Christchurch, Canterbury, is dominated philosophically by the [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") denomination.

Originally there were two branches of Presbyterianism in New Zealand, the northern Presbyterian church which existed in the North Island and the parts of the South Island north of the [Waitaki River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitaki_River "Waitaki River"), and the [Synod of Otago and Southland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod_of_Otago_and_Southland "Synod of Otago and Southland"), founded by [Free Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Church_of_Scotland_/(1843%E2%80%931900/) "Free Church of Scotland (1843–1900)") settlers in southern South Island. The two churches merged in 1901, forming what is now the [Presbyterian Church of Aotearoa New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Presbyterian Church of Aotearoa New Zealand").

In addition to the Presbyterian Church of Aotearoa New Zealand, there is also a more conservative Presbyterian church called [Grace Presbyterian Church of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Presbyterian_Church_of_New_Zealand "Grace Presbyterian Church of New Zealand"). Many of its members left the largely liberal PCANZ because they were seeking a more conservative church. It has 17 churches throughout New Zealand.

In [Vanuatu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanuatu "Vanuatu"), the [Presbyterian Church in Vanuatu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_Vanuatu "Presbyterian Church in Vanuatu") is the largest denomination in the country, with approximately one-third of the population of Vanuatu members of the church. The PCV was taken to Vanuatu by missionaries from Scotland. The PCV (Presbyterian Church in Vanuatu) is headed by a moderator with offices in [Port Vila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Vila "Port Vila"). The PCV is particularly strong in the provinces of [Tafea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tafea "Tafea"), [Shefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shefa_Province "Shefa Province"), and [Malampa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malampa "Malampa"). The Province of [Sanma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanma_Province "Sanma Province") is mainly Presbyterian with a strong Catholic minority in the [Francophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francophone "Francophone") areas of the province. There are some Presbyterian people, but no organised Presbyterian churches in [Penama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penama "Penama") and [Torba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torba_Province "Torba Province"), both of which are traditionally Anglican. Vanuatu is the only country in the South Pacific with a significant Presbyterian heritage and membership. The PCV is a founding member of yjr Vanuatu Christian Council (VCC). The PCV runs many primary schools and Onesua secondary school. The church is strong in the rural villages.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| 
The Engagers



 |
| --- |
| [![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG/330px-17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG)

A Covenanter's helmet from the period in the [Museum of Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Edinburgh "Museum of Edinburgh")



 |
| Founded | December 1647 |
| Dissolved | 1651 |
| Split from | [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters") |
| Religion | [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") ([Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland")) |
| 

*   [Politics of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Scotland "Politics of Scotland")
*   [Political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Scotland "List of political parties in Scotland")
*   [Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Scotland "Elections in Scotland")



 |

The **Engagers** were a faction of the [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"), who made "**The Engagement**" with King [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") in December 1647 while he was imprisoned in [Carisbrooke Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle") by the [English Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Parliamentarians "English Parliamentarians") after his defeat in the [First Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War").

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg/250px-The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)

The [Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed by English and Scottish Presbyterians in 1643

In the 17th and 18th centuries, politics and religion were closely linked; it is impossible to understand differences between Engagers, Royalists or [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") political views without an appreciation of these distinctions.

'[Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity")' versus '[Episcopalian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity")' implied differences in governance, not [doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctrine "Doctrine"). Episcopalian meant rule by bishops, appointed by the monarch; Presbyterian structures were controlled by [Elders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elder_/(Christianity/) "Elder (Christianity)"), nominated by their congregations. Arguments over structure or governance of the church were as much about politics and the power of the monarch as religious practice; political divisions often centred on different interpretations of this.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-1)

The [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation") created a [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"), or 'kirk', Presbyterian in structure and governance, and predominantly [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism") in doctrine. When [James VI and I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") became king of England in 1603, a unified Church of Scotland and England governed by bishops became the first step in his vision of a centralised, Unionist state.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStephen201055%E2%80%9358-2) Although both churches were nominally Episcopalian, they were very different in doctrine; even bishops in Scotland viewed many [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") practices as little better than Catholicism.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonald199875%E2%80%9376-3)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg/250px-1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)

[James Graham, Marquis of Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose"); Royalist commander in Scotland 1644–1645, but a Covenanter general 1638 to 1640

Efforts by [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") to impose uniform practices led to the 1638 [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant"), whose signatories pledged to resist liturgical 'innovations'. In December 1638, bishops were expelled from the kirk; when Charles attempted to use military force, he was defeated in the 1639 and 1640 [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), which left the [Covenanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter "Covenanter") party in control of Scotland.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackieLenmanParker1986204%E2%80%93205-4)

Calvinists believed a 'well-ordered' monarchy was part of God's plan; as a result, the vast majority of Covenanters agreed monarchy itself was divinely ordered but disagreed on who held ultimate authority in clerical affairs.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacleod20095%E2%80%9319_passim-5) Royalists and Engagers tended to argue the king held supreme authority, but that did not necessarily mean they supported bishops and individual motives were very complex. Many fought for both Covenant and king at different times, including [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201553%E2%80%9354-6)

When the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") began in 1642, Scotland initially remained neutral, but became involved in the [Irish Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"); the bitterness of this conflict radicalised views in Scotland and Ireland.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005142-7) The Covenanter faction known as the [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"), led by [Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), saw religious union with England as the best way to preserve a Presbyterian kirk and in October 1643 the [Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed a Presbyterian Union in return for Scottish military support.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertson2014125-8)

Royalists and moderates in both Scotland and England opposed union, as did the religious [Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_/(religion/) "Independent (religion)") like [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), who dominated the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") and opposed any state-ordered church. Both Covenanters and their English allies saw the Independents as a bigger threat than the Royalists and when Charles surrendered in 1646, they began negotiations to restore him to the English throne.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005420%C2%B7423-9)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg/250px-The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)

[Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), whose [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") opposed the Engagement

The Scots nominated three Commissioners to negotiate with Charles; [Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Maitland,_1st_Duke_of_Lauderdale "John Maitland, 1st Duke of Lauderdale"), [Lanark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton") and [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Campbell,_1st_Earl_of_Loudoun "John Campbell, 1st Earl of Loudoun"). In December 1647, Charles agreed to impose Presbyterianism in England for three years and suppress the Independents, but his refusal to take the Covenant himself split the Scots.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-10) It was not until April 1648 the Engagers achieved a majority in the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland"); Argyll's Kirk Party did not trust Charles, objected to an alliance with English and Scots Royalists, and denounced the Engagement as 'sinful.'[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitchisonFryFry2002223%E2%80%93224-11)

Most of the Scottish army had been demobilised and efforts to recruit new regiments were undermined when many refused to serve, including their most experienced generals, [Lord Leven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie,_1st_Earl_of_Leven "Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven") and [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_/(Scottish_general/) "David Leslie (Scottish general)"). The inexperienced [Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton") was given command, with the [Earl of Callendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Livingston,_1st_Earl_of_Callendar "James Livingston, 1st Earl of Callendar") as his subordinate. When deputy to Leven, Callendar's overestimation of his military abilities had led to constant conflict and this was repeated with Hamilton. His commander of infantry, [William Baillie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Baillie_/(soldier/) "William Baillie (soldier)"), had direct experience of the New Model Army and doubted their ability to defeat it.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005424-12)

After dispersing Kirk Party dissidents at [Mauchline Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir "Battle of Mauchline Muir") in June 1648, a poorly trained Engager army of 9,000 marched into England. The [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") was intended as a series of Royalist risings in England and Wales, with the Scots providing support. By the time Hamilton's army entered [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire") in early August, the other revolts had been suppressed and Cromwell routed the Engagers at [Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_/(1648/) "Battle of Preston (1648)") on 19 August. Hamilton was taken prisoner and executed in March 1649.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

Defeat at Preston led to the collapse of the Engager regime; the Kirk Party took control of [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and although repulsed at [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stirling_/(1648/) "Battle of Stirling (1648)") in September, a new civil war seemed imminent. However, with Cromwell's support, Argyll took control and expelled his Engager opponents, with English troops being withdrawn.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

The 1649 [Act of Classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Classes "Act of Classes") banned Engagers and Royalists from holding political or military office and established the Kirk Party as the government of Scotland. However, the execution of Charles in January 1649 was viewed by Covenanters as an offence against God; they proclaimed his son [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") King of Scotland and Great Britain. In the 1650 [Treaty of Breda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Breda_/(1650/) "Treaty of Breda (1650)"), they agreed to restore Charles to the English throne; in return he accepted the Covenant. Defeats by Cromwell at [Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dunbar_/(1650/) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)") and [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") resulted in Scotland being incorporated into the [Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England,_Scotland_and_Ireland "Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland") in 1654.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005520-14)

The siege and [battle of Colchester](https://sevenswords.uk/english-civil-war-every-battle/) in 1648 marked a moment when the already frayed nerves of England finally snapped. It was a long, grinding struggle in a walled town that did not particularly want to be a stage for national collapse yet found itself swept up in the storm. As a historian, I find Colchester fascinating because it shows the Civil War at its most stubborn. No grand cavalry sweeps, no dashing charges, just hard sieges, hunger, and the slow cracking of a Royalist last stand. At times it feels less like a battlefield and more like a tragic civic marathon.

By the summer of 1648 the Second English Civil War was underway and Colchester found itself held by a Royalist force that had failed to secure wider support. Parliament’s New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax arrived, and there began a brutal siege lasting eleven weeks. The Royalists under Sir Charles Lucas and Sir George Lisle refused to surrender despite starvation and hopeless odds. Their stand turned Colchester into one of the most poignant final acts of the Royalist cause.

* * *

A clear view of the opposing forces helps frame the scale and strain of the siege.

Parliamentarian Forces
----------------------

| Commander | Notes | Estimated Strength |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sir Thomas Fairfax | Commander in Chief of the New Model Army | About 5,000 to 6,000 |
| Thomas Rainsborough | Senior officer, naval links, rising political figure | Part of Fairfax’s command |
| John Lambert | Leading cavalry commander | Detached elements present |

Royalist Forces
---------------

| Commander | Notes | Estimated Strength |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sir Charles Lucas | Local and respected Royalist officer | About 4,000 |
| Sir George Lisle | Veteran commander | Senior leadership |
| Lord Capel | Noble supporter providing legitimacy | Civic influence rather than numbers |

* * *

Arms And Armour
---------------

A detailed look at what both sides carried into this grinding siege.

Parliamentarian Equipment
-------------------------

| Unit Type | Arms | Armour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New Model Infantry | Matchlock muskets, pikes, mortars for siege bombardment, side arms such as [mortuary swords](https://sevenswords.uk/the-mortuary-sword/) | Buff coats, iron helmets, breastplates for pikemen |
| Cavalry | Pistols, carbines, backswords of the mortuary and hanger types | Lobster-tailed pot helmets, cuirass front and back |
| Artillery | Demi-culverins, sakers, mortars | Minimal armour, leather aprons |

**Parliamentarian Sword Types**  
• Mortuary sword with stylised hilt masks  
• Backsword with single edged blade for cavalry  
• Infantry hangers often used for siege work and close encounters

Royalist Equipment
------------------

| Unit Type | Arms | Armour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Infantry | Matchlocks, pikes, shorter wheel-lock pistols among officers | Mixed armour due to supply shortages |
| Cavalry | Cavalry swords often of Walloon type, pistols | Three quarter armour in some elite units, but increasingly rare |
| Garrison Artillery | Old demi-culverins and falconets on the walls | Limited armour |

**Royalist Sword Types**  
• Walloon swords with shell guards  
• Cavalry sabres of continental influence  
• Officer’s rapiers, especially among senior gentlemen

* * *

Leaders And Troop Composition
-----------------------------

Parliamentarian Highlights
--------------------------

• Veteran New Model regiments with hard discipline  
• Strong artillery corps well supplied  
• Cohesive command structure under Fairfax

Royalist Highlights
-------------------

• Mixed force of veterans and local retainers  
• Officers of high rank but lacking unity  
• Insufficient artillery and dwindling supplies

* * *

The Siege And Battle
--------------------

Colchester’s walls were old but serviceable. The Royalists hoped for relief forces that never materialised. Fairfax settled in for a professional siege. Trenches crept toward the town. Artillery chipped away at defences. Food ran thin inside and desperate measures followed. Accounts of horses, dogs, and even candles being eaten are grim reminders that the war was unforgiving to civilians.

Parliament’s lines tightened until Colchester was strangled. The Royalist leaders refused surrender again and again, even while their men starved. When the inevitable came in late August, Fairfax accepted a negotiated surrender for the rank and file but refused clemency for Lucas and Lisle, who were executed shortly afterwards just outside the town. Their deaths shocked contemporaries, although the Parliamentarian leadership viewed them as necessary examples. History still debates whether they were martyrs, fools, or simply men who had run out of options.

* * *

Contemporary Quotes
-------------------

Sir Thomas Fairfax, writing during the siege:  
_“We are resolved to endure the labour until the town submit, for the safety of the kingdom demands no less.”_

A Royalist letter smuggled from Colchester:  
_“Our bellies grow light, but our hearts must grow heavier still, yet honour forbids that we yield.”_

A Parliamentarian soldier’s diary:  
_“Colchester stands by stubbornness alone, for its walls are less strong than the wills of those within.”_

* * *

Archaeology
-----------

Colchester has always been generous to archaeologists and the siege left its own fingerprints. Excavations around the Balkerne Gate and St Mary’s area have revealed musket balls flattened on impact, fragments of mortar shells, and buckles from soldiers’ kit. There are also signs of emergency slaughter pits that match written accounts of the town’s desperate food shortage.

The most evocative finds are small personal items, from buttons to knife handles, reminders that the siege was a human experience before it became a historical one. Some musket balls appear to have been improvised from scrap lead, suggesting that ammunition supplies inside the town were collapsing in the final weeks.

* * *

Battle Timeline
---------------

**May 1648**  
Royalist forces take Colchester, hoping to rally wider support.

**13 June 1648**  
Fairfax marches on the town and battle skirmishes begin outside the walls.

**14 June 1648**  
Full siege begins, with Parliamentarian lines closing off escape or supply.

**June to July 1648**  
Artillery bombardments, trench approaches, and worsening starvation inside the walls.

**Early August 1648**  
Failed Royalist attempts to hold out for relief. Conditions deteriorate rapidly.

**28 August 1648**  
Colchester surrenders.

**Immediately After**  
Lucas and Lisle executed. Parliament reasserts control in the region.

* * *

Legacy
------

The fall of Colchester effectively broke the remaining Royalist resistance in the Second Civil War. The severity of the siege and the execution of Lucas and Lisle left wounds that lingered for generations. Even today the site of their deaths, the so called Dead Man’s Tree, has become part of the town’s identity. As a historian I find Colchester important because it reveals the Civil War’s transformation from grand ideals to the weary grind of attrition. By 1648 the conflict had lost any romantic veneer and had become a matter of survival, principle, and stubbornness.

Marmaduke Langdale, first Baron Langdale (?1598-1661)
-----------------------------------------------------

Royalist cavalry general during the [Civil War](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/wars_ecw1.html). As High Sheriff of Yorkshire he opposed [Charles I's](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/people_charlesI.html) [ship money](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/concepts_shipmoney.html), but when war came he joined the Royalist cause. As the war wore on, he came increasingly to the fore. He was present at [Marston Moor (2 July 1644)](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/battles_marston_moor.html), and after the defeat managed to bring back together his scattered cavalry, leaving York with [Prince Rupert](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/people_prince_rupert.html) (4 July 1644). Early in 1645, he re-entered Yorkshire with a flying column of cavalry, managing to relieve the siege of Pontefract (1 March 1645), one of the few Royalist successes at this time. In May, he joined Charles I's field army at Ashby de la Zouch. At the end of the month he cut off the Parliamentary garrison of Leicester, in preparation for the arrival of Prince Rupert with the main army (29 May), which quickly resulted in the surrender of the city. Like many Royalist commanders, his control over his men was not perfect, and on 4 June when the Royalist army prepared to move south to seek out [Fairfax](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/people_fairfax.html), his cavalry refused to march, and headed to Newark, but he soon regained control,. and at [Naseby (14 June 1645)](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/battles_naseby.html), his 1,600 strong northern horse formed the Royalist left flank, facing [Cromwell's](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/people_cromwell.html) [Ironsides](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/weapons_ironsides.html), who outnumbered them. This was to prove important in the battle. Despite fighting well, Langdale was soon driven off the battlefield, and Cromwell had enough spare cavalry to make sure he could not rally his troups and return to the fray. However, he was soon able to regroup, and rejoin Charles in the aftermath of the battle, when Charles decided to march to Scotland. However, this plan too failed. As the Royalist force approached Chester, it was clear that they would have to act to save the city, the loss of which would cut off any hope of reinforcements from Ireland. Langdale, with 3,000 cavalry, moved to attack the Parliamentary forces, but he was intercepted by General Poyntz, ([Battle of Rowton Heath, 24 September 1645](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/battles_rowtonheath.html)), with an equal force of cavalry. After an initial fight early in the day, the two sides were in stalemate, neither able to move, until Poyntz managed to get reinforcements from the besieging forces. Langdale was now in a very poor position, and an attempt to reach safety in Chester failed, leaving Charles helpless to help as his cavalry were cut down beneath the walls, eventually fleeing.Langdale next surfaced in the [Second Civil War](https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/wars_ecw2.html). On 28 April 1648 he captured Berwick for the King, and joined the Scottish army on it's march south. By mid-August, the Scottish army was close to Preston (Lancs), with Cromwell close by. Of the Royalist commanders, only Langdale realised that the main Parliamentary army was close by, but could not convince his superiors of this, and on the first day of the battle of Preston (17-19 August 1648), he was left to face the entire enemy army unaided. Unsurprisingly, his force was overwhelmed, although he managed to escape the field. He was temporarily taken prisoner at Nottingham, but managed to escape again, and reaching the continent, where he eventually reached Venice. On the restoration he returned to England, and in 1658 was created Baron Langdale by Charles II for his role in the war. His troops were better controlled than most on the Royalist side, but he was unfortunate enough to be present at a series of Royalist defeats.

#### [Books on the English Civil War](https://www.historyofwar.org/bookshop/books_ecw.html) | [Subject Index: English Civil War](https://www.historyofwar.org/subject_english_civil_war.html)

**How to cite this article:** Rickard, J. (1 April 2001), _Marmaduke Langdale, first Baron Langdale (?1598-1661)_, https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/people\_langdale.html
